maintopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if I am within the. rules I should like to say a few words about the formation of this committee that the government proposes to establish. In his speech yesterday the Prime Minister spoke at some length and offered the suggestion that Wednesday sittings be done away with in order to give members the opportunity to do more work on committees, and also to give more time to the members of the cabinet to look after their very important work. What I want to know is this: how are the members who are not members of the committees to make the contribution they should like to make in order to help the administration of the country? On February 22 of last year I suggested that members from the province of Quebec opposing the government should be given places on those important committees, but my suggestion was turned down. If we are to take it for granted that the opposition should be represented on all committees that have to do with important matters affecting the country, then I suppose, according to the same principle, members from the province of Quebec who in this house are opposing the government should be given the opportunity to make their contribution and bring their views to those committees. Therefore, if my request is in order, I would ask that opposition members from the province of Quebec be nominated to the important committees that the government intends to establish before long.

maintopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand this motion is debatable, and I desire to say a word in reference to it. I had the honour of serving on a committee which in 1928 revised the rules of this house under the chairmanship of Mr. Speaker Lemieux, with the help, as a friend of the court, of the present Clerk of the House of Commons. We thought we had done a pretty good job at that time. I regret that the country as a whole, as I understand it, now thinks there were some grave errors and omissions in the work of that committee. I agree that as a result of the demand of public opinion the whole position should be reexamined, and I am glad that the Prime Minister has brought forward this motion.
I sympathize to some extent with the point of view of the hon. gentleman who has just spoken (Mr. Roy), but in connection with a matter of this kind I fear a large committee would not be as effective as a small one. I hope that while there may be some disadvantage-none is apparent to me, at all events-the Prime Minister will adhere to the principle of a small committee. I think it can do more effective and more continuous work than a large committee.
The position taken by the hon. member for Gaspe illustrates what is taking place in this house with a multiplicity of parties. We do not need to tell members of this house what difficult situations arise as a result, but such is democracy and- we have to meet it. At the same time a situation of this kind, which has to do with the internal economy of the house, makes it impossible to give representation to every political party that springs up ephemerally, and temporarily I hope, in this House of Commons. Therefore I am going to support the motion as put, in the hope that useful work will be done by this committee, but without any great 'hope that there will evolve any revolutionary departure from the rules; because after all this is the people's parliament, the high court of Canada, a deliberative assembly wherein the people's representatives meet to express the point of view of those who have sent -them here, and I strongly deprecate the curtailment of the right of free speech.

maintopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to say a word or two in respect of the motion before us, may I make an observation or two which I believe will represent the sentiment of a good many of those who sit in this house. I am in support of the motion, but I believe if all the committee does is to readjust a few minor rules, the full importance of the committee's work will not be realized. I fancy it makes very

War Appropriation
little difference whether or not a member is permitted to speak half an hour or forty minutes, or whether or hot we sit on Wednesdays, or whether or not certain language may or may not be used, and the rules and regulations adjusted accordingly. I should like to see the terms of reference extended in order that a more complete democratic form of parliamentary procedure may be brought about. I appreciate what the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) said when he pointed out that this is the people's parliament. That may be true in theory, Mr. Speaker, but it is not true in practice. We all represent the people, but because of certain party affiliations we can only act as a sort of sounding board, and when votes are taken it does not make very much difference what the people's representatives say.
I believe that the terms of reference to this committee should be extended to look into the matter I have just referred to. The government of this country should be the servants of the people; they should be the servants of parliament. They are not. We cannot vote along certain lines for fear that the vote may be interpreted as a vote of want of confidence, upon which the government would resign. I do not think that should be so in our parliamentary practice. I think we should be free to vote in whatever way we desire, and the government should become the administrative body to put into effect what parliament desires. It does not work that way in practice, as we know; the government seems to be the big boss of the representatives of the people. I wish the work of the committee could be extended in order to place this parliament upon a more practical basis as representing the will of the people, so that the government would become the administrative body to put into operation that which the representatives of the people desire.

maintopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, the text of the resolution does not go far enough. This committee should consider the whole question of parliamentary, constitutional, cabinet and law reform. After all is said and done we are now in the fifth year of the war, and parliament has to do very little work indeed. We have appointed outside boards and commissions to such an extent that we have abrogated the functions of parliament, and the so-called supremacy of parliament has become a myth. I believe that with all these controls there is very little business for parliament to do except the holding of post mortems; the money is spent before the estimates reach this house. I believe the work to be done by this committee should embrace the subjects I have 100-5
mentioned. If we had a rule similar to that of the British parliament, under which on the orders of the day supplementary questions might be asked, five-sixths of the debates in this house would be eliminated.

maintopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: I should like this committee to consider the suggestion that when the hour of worship is called here the general public should be'welcomed. This is the only place in Canada, so far as I know, where the doors are locked against the general public wrhen we meet together for the worship of God. Surely the general public need it as much as we do.
Motion agreed to.

speakeroldname: Hon. N. A. McLARTY (Secretary of State) moved:
subtopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON TAKING OF VOTE OF ACTIVE SERVICE FORCES
SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON TAKING OF VOTE OF ACTIVE SERVICE FORCES
speechtext:
Replying to the first part s>f the question of the leader of the opposition,

I may say that the regulations governing the 1940 general election Were passed under the War Measures Act. My hon. friend will remember that there was not a very lengthy session of parliament in that year, and consequently such regulations could not be considered by this house. I am advised and believe, from the fact that no complaints were received at that time, that the procedure then adopted worked satisfactorily and well. However, conditions have greatly changed since then. In the first place the number serving in the armed forces has increased very substantially, and they are widely dispersed all over the world. The government is anxious that the fullest opportunity be given those serving in the armed forces to exercise their franchise in the selection of those whom they wish to represent them in parliament. That is the whole purpose of the motion, and perhaps this statement of government policy will answer the second portion of my hon. friend's question.

subtopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON TAKING OF VOTE OF ACTIVE SERVICE FORCES
speechtext: In other words I take it that there will be no proxy system in the next general election?

subtopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON TAKING OF VOTE OF ACTIVE SERVICE FORCES
speechtext: I think it would be a little unfair to tie the hands of the committee. The regulations which have been drafted by the chief electoral officer with the collaboration of Mr. Harry Butcher, a former member of this house who served on the committee which sat in 1937 and 1938, and who I believe enjoys the esteem of all hon. members of this house, will be submitted to the committee for consideration, and I suggest that at this time it would be unwise to endeavour in any way to tie the hands of the committee by making any commitment as to the particular procedure which might be followed.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. G. POWER (Minister of National Defence for Air):
speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON TAKING OF VOTE OF ACTIVE SERVICE FORCES
speechtext:
Perhaps I may say a word, since I was to some extent responsible for drafting the regulations governing service voting in 1940. I should like to point out to the house that these regulations will be somewhat more difficult of application under present circumstances. For instance, referring only to the Royal Canadian Air Force, in 1940 there were something like five hundred of the personnel of the air force overseas. At the present time it runs closer to fifty or sixty thousand, and they are widely dispersed over every part of the globe. So that the machinery which was set up in 1940, which I think all parties agreed was reasonably efficient and which at one time was almost unanimously considered by the house and the country to be fair and reasonable, will have to be considerably modified and altered.

Dominion Elections
Then other suggestions have been made with respect to the methods and manner of taking the vote. For instance there has been a suggestion made, one which I saw in a fairly widely publicized book by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) that the members of the forces should be represented in this house by members of parliament at large, a certain number of members elected over and above the 245 for which the constitution provides. Of course that presupposes a constitutional amendment. Also, if I may say so-and I am not prepared at the moment to discuss the question on its merits-it comes perilously close to the fascist system, the corporative form of government, so close, in fact, that I am astonished to find my hon. friend promoting it.
It has some disadvantages, and from the standpoint of draftsmanship great advantages. The drafting of the legislation certainly would be easier if we were simply to say that the members of the aimed forces serving overseas would be represented by, let us say, one member for every 20,000, 30,000 or 40,000 as the case may be. As a matter of fact I am informed that in the last war the province of Saskatchewan did have three members at large, one of whom was for Canada, one for' Great Britain and one for France. So that the mechanics of that method would be comparatively easy. It would be very easy to make a provision whereby any, we will say, twenty-five members of the forces could nominate any other member of those forces, and after being duly certified as being a member of such unit he would be a candidate. I presume the whole 200,000 or 300,000 soldiers would vote for a certain number of candidates at large, each having the right to vote for ten or twenty members, as the case might be. So that from the point of view of mechanics or draftsmanship, if I had anything to do with the drafting I would welcome it. But I do not know that the country as a whole would support the setting up of a sort of military caste of some twenty or thirty members, in addition to those for whom provision is already made in our constitution. Nor perhaps would the men themselves like to be deprived of their right to vote in the constituency in which (hey had formerly voted. I suggest this procedure is something which might be studied by the committee. I bring these points forward so that they may be called to the attention of members of the house. The regulations made in 1940 are not in themselves perfect. They will have to be modified and amended, and any other method ought at least to be considered.
100-5J
There is a further suggestion-and again from the standpoint of mechanics or draftsmanship, it probably presents even greater facilities than any of the others, and it has to do with all due respect to my hon. friend the acting leader of the opposition (Mr. Gray-don), with a sort of proxy system. The suggestion I received was that the regulations called for the right of every member of the forces to vote by proxy, and automatically that there should be inscribed on the electoral lists of the appropriate riding or electoral constituency wherein the next of kin reside, the name of the service man, with the designated next of kin as proxy. This has been explained to me only vaguely, but it would work out something like this: Tom Jones resides on Metcalfe street, Ottawa. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a question to the Minister of Agriculture based on a press release of January 22, which recites the intention of the government to pay a premium of $3 on grade A carcasses of hogs and a premium of S2 on carcasses of grade B-l. The next sentence is ambiguous and capable of two or three interpretations. The fact that this premium is already in operation is my reason for asking the question on the orders of the day rather than putting it on the order paper, because I have had many inquiries about it. The sentence to which I refer reads:
The premium of $1 formerly paid by the packers on grade A carcasses will be paid on the carcass grade value for export bacon.
This has created some confusion. I would ask the minister, first, whether it is intended that this premium of SI on grade A carcasses should be paid by the packers or by the government? Second, will the premium be paid on all grade A carcasses or only on such carcasses as are exported?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
maintopic: INQUIRY WITH REFERENCE TO PREMIUM ON GRADE A AND GRADE B-l CARCASSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the present position is that the plan as announced on the 22nd of January is in substitution for one not yet put into effect. The announcement previously made indicated that it would take two or three weeks to get the plan worked out, but we

The Address-Mr. Roebuck
found within a few days that there was going to be so much difficulty in meeting the situation with regard to individual farmers if something were not done immediately, that on January 22 we asked the packing plants and others who were taking deliveries of hogs to make payment of the premium of $3 on A's and $2 on B-l's when deliveries were made as from the next Monday morning. But at the same time we indicated that the SI premium which had been previously paid on A's will not be paid after the final set-up is made. In the meantime the SI premium is being paid by the packing plants and other purchasers of grade A hogs. But after the plan is set up, it is intended that the SI premium will be spread over the two classifications, A's and B-l's, which are the export grades, in some proportion which will be reasonable in relation to the value of A's as compared with B's. Then there will be an A price and a B price, as well as prices on grades below. The premiums of $3 and S2 will be paid by the government only on A's and B-l's. The present intention is that they will be paid in the form of a warrant which will be attached to the cheque which the farmer receives for his hogs so that he will be able to take it to the bank and cash it along with his cheque.

speechtext: The house resumed from Monday, January 31, consideration of the motion of Mr. L. D. Tremblay' for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Graydon, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Coldwell.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I, notwithstanding the well-chosen words-perhaps I might borrow the adjectives of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and say the amiable words of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Graydon) in reference to the form of this debate-nevertheless conform to the ancient and delightful parliamentary custom of offering felicitations to the mover (Mr. Tremblay) and the seconder (Mr. Tucker) of the address. It was an excellent custom, and they were excellent addresses. But I should like to go further than is dictated by ancient custom and offer a word of commendation and compliment in respect to all the addresses which have preceded mine. They were all good addresses. And why not? Why should they not be good addresses? Eveiy one of them was delivered by the leader of a political party, six or seven of them, and of course, with the status of leadership conferred upon the individual, one would expect that his speech would be broad in scope, well delivered, and so forth.
The Lon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) has just now referred to the multiplicity of parties, and I am wondering, Mr. Speaker, if the time will not shortly arrive, in the course of the political development which is now on our hands, when we will all be leaders of a political party. Two hundred and forty-five of us, each leading his own party, would surely improve the quality of the debates and we could adopt as our motto "Every man his own leader".
I have observed in the addresses of all the leaders who have spoken so far-some of them leaders of parties of one, but nevertheless leaders-a certain delightful and inspiring flavour of international politics. I cannot say whether that is the result of the status of leadership, or whether it comes from the divinity that doth hedge a king, or what it is. But I have noticed it with a great deal of interest. Or perhaps it was the evidence that I saw in these addresses of the growing importance of this assembly and the recognition of the fact that we who sit here are representative of a nation-Canada's status within the family of nations. I hope that is so.
Not being myself a leader but just one of the rank and file of the common people, I of course can accept a statement of policy laid down by somebody else; and so I wish to say that I approve very highly the statesmanlike pronouncement which was made in this house yesterday afternoon by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). It is in my judgment a sufficient answer to the question propounded by the noble lord from across the sea as to the future of Canada within the commonwealth of nations and in the world at large.
There was a time in this country when politicians and rank and file were prepared to accept their international thinking from titled gentlemen in Downing Street, and there are still, Mr. Speaker, some colonial-minded people in Canada. We have been slow, very slow, in
The Address-Mr. Roebuck

benefited from these activities. Nevertheless, riots, disorder and violence have characterized the conduct of the Arab majority ever since the emigracion began. In 1937, due to the violence of the Arabs, a proposal was made to partition Palestine into two states, one Jewish and the other Arab, but it was rejected by both sides as impracticable. Then in 1938, after a conference in London of both Jewish and Arab representatives failed to reach some compromise agreement, the British government brought down what is known as the Chamberlain white paper. Some of the facts set out in that white paper are interesting. It says:
Since the statement of 1922 was published, more than 300,000 Jews have immigrated to Palestine, and the population of the national home has risen to some 450,000, or approaching a third of the entire population of the country. Nor has the Jewish community failed to take full advantage of the opportunity given to it. The growth of the national home and its achievement in many fields are a remarkably constructive effort which must command the admiration of the world and must be, in particular, a source of pride to Jewish people.
Then a little further:
The methods employed by Arab terrorists, against fellow Arabs and Jews alike must
receive unqualified condemnation.
Those are the facts set out in the Chamberlain white paper; yet in the face of those facts and for purely political reasons- I mean "political" in its widest sense-this is the statement of policy which follows:
Jewish immigration during the next five years will be at a rate which, if economic absorptive capacity admits, will bring the Jewish population up to approximately one-third of the total population of the country.
And the next paragraph:
After a period of five years no further Jewish immigration will be permitted unless the Arabs of Palestine are prepared to acquiesce in it.
I submit to this house that this is the most perfect example of Chamberlain appeasement one could well imagine. It is appeasement in this, that it submits to the very violence which it condemns. It is appeasement in that it not only submits to the violence of the violent but it does so at the expense of the innocent. That, I take it, is Chamberlain appeasement at its worst.
I am not the only one who holds these views, or who has raised his voice in protest in regard to what is expected to happen at the end of next month. The matter was debated in the British House of Commons shortly after the paper was issued in 1939. At that time, referring to this provision that there shall be no more immigration into Pales-
[Mr. Roebuck.!
tine without the acquiescence of the Arabs, Right Hon. Winston Churchill made this statement:
Now, there is the breach; there is the violation of the pledge; there is the abandonment of the Balfour declaration; there is the end of the vision, of the hope, of the dream.
Mr. Amery, who was a member of the war cabinet at the time the Balfour declaration was issued and was later colonial secretary, made this reference:
It is a repudiation of the pledge on the strength of which the government of Palestine was entrusted to our hands.
In the House of Lords the Right Reverend Cosmo Gordon Lang, Archbishop of Canterbury, made a denunciation practically as strong. He said:
If the Arabs are willing to allow an extension over that one-third of the population, another of the wonders of the world will have occurred. The position therefore is that the Jews are reduced to the status of a permanent minority. I venture to think that it was precisely from this permanent minority that they hoped to escape.
You may ask why Canada is especially interested in this problem of Palestine. In part my answer has been given already. In this country there are from 150,000 to 200,000 Jewish people, and the Zionist Organization of Canada has actually invested in Palestine an amount estimated in the neighbourhood of $5,000,000, in addition to the private subscriptions to various industrial and agricultural enterprises. This $5,000,000 was invested by the Zionist Organization on the strength of its members' faith in the Balfour declaration. We in Canada have a right to demand fair play and justice to our own investors.
In addition, of the twelve million Jewish people outside the axis countries, about one and a half million are in the armies of the united nations. Even in Canada, with our smaller population and much smaller army, we have some 14,000 Jewish boys under arms. I submit that this house, this nation and the allied nations as a whole must keep faith with these men.
Furthermore, Canada is a member of the league of nations; and so I hark back to what I have said: with power there goes responsibility. With responsibility there is sometimes call for action. Canada is a member of the organization which gave to Great Britain her mandate over Palestine. Accordingly, Canada has a right to point out, if she so desires, that the white paper is noit a proper and just rendering of the Balfour declaration, and that, as a practical matter, the closing of the doors of Palestine against one of these large branches of the refugee group is not in the

. o
The Address-Mr. Adamson
best interests of the world at large, is not a Christian act, or a statesmanlike act. Canada is to-day a world power. She can no longer stand aside accepting the immunities of childhood in an adult world.
Our own position in connection with refugee emigration is not such as to provide a salve for an injured conscience. I have already said that some 3,500,000 Jewish people have been murdered by the nazi butchers, within those areas controlled by Hitler and his gang. Of that number 1,500,000 are scattered to the four winds. May I ask this question: How many of this group of refugees have found refuge on the soil of Canada? The last figures available, those for 1942, show a grand total of Hebrew immigration into Canada for the year ending March 31 of that year of 111 persons. That includes men, women and children. I draw attention to this figure of 111 persons out of the 1,500,000 scattered by Hitler.
Of course all the 111 were not refugees. That is the total of Hebrew immigration or, to be more exact, immigrants who professed the Hebrew religion. In the year before the number was 284. Surely in Canada, with our great heritage of 3,500,000 square miles of territory, we have room for more than one or two hundred persecuted people fleeing for their lives from nazi butchers. I should think we could have found a space in this great heritage to extend a helping hand to more than 111 of such people, or rather that portion of the 111 who were actually Jewish refugees.
At the outbreak of war Canada deliberately and purposely closed her immigration offices in Europe and, I believe, in Asia. The one exception was the office in London, England. We also withdrew our immigration officials. I am delighted to note that within the last two or three months we have reopened our immigration office in Lisbon, Portugal, and the immigration officer there has been charged, I believe, with the responsibility of devising methods of carrying out programmes of relief and help. I do not know what the returns are, because I have seen nothing published about his activities. I have been told, however, that Canada has offered to extend a helping hand to some few of those refugees who have found asylum in Portgual, but that so far as the Jewish immigrants are concerned they preferred to go on to Palestine, where the door is still open, and may continue to be open for a short time after March 31.
I say that because in a debate in the British House of Commons in November of 1942, the colonial secretary gave assurance that the full number of 75,000 immigrants would be permitted as had been promised by the Chamber-100- 6 J
lain white paper, notwithstanding the passing of the exact date. And so the gates of Palestine are not yet closed. I am hopeful that an expression of opinion, even so humble as mine, coupled with many othef such expressions, may result in a reconsideration of this subject, and that Canada may make representations along the lines I have suggested. I am encouraged in that thought by the statement by Lord Halifax, speaking in Washington on January 17 of this year, on which occasion he expressed a doubt as to whether Great Britain would actually carry out the formal declaration of the white paper and close the gates of Palestine on March 31. It would seem therefore that the situation is not hopless- indeed, far from it. It is my view that were public opinion aroused in Canada, and that were our government to express, even in the mildest of terms, some of the thoughts I have v*oiced, as Churchill has put it, the vision, the hope and the dream of a national home in Palestine for the descendants of the writers of the Bible may yet be preserved.
Since in my opinion the opening of an immigration office in Lisbon was in response to an awakening public conscience, so do I hope that a further awakening may lead to Canada's still further liberalizing her immigration, policy. I am not advocating that the immigration bars be thrown down, because that is no longer possible in the world as we know it to-day. But aside from the immigration problem, I do believe that Canada should, and I hope will, extend a hand, along with other Christian nations of the world, with a view to saving as many as possible from the fury of the nazi butchers.

I shall have more to say on this a little later but the hon. member for Trinity gave me the opportunity of saying a few words now.
The Address-Mr. Adamson

When I listened yesterday to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) expound the theme of the supremacy of parliament I thought of some other places where his remarks, instead of being received with the adulation of a mechanical majority, would have brought forth active and violent signs of derision and displeasure. The theory of parliamentary supremacy is all important to the future of the country, because a docile parliament subservient to the rule of the leader has always been the first step to the loss of individual freedom, to dictatorship, and eventually to revolution. That is the danger to-day in Canada, and nowhere is it more evident than in the smoke-screen which is the speech from the throne.
To say that the speech from the throne recognizes the importance of the war is theoretically correct. It recognizes the importance of the war in exactly the same way as the president of a great corporation recognizes the loyalty of the employees in his annual report. In other words, he does it in a stereotyped paragraph, thanking them for their work during the past year and hoping that they will continue to show the same commendable consideration in the future.
Great concern was expressed yesterday by the Prime Minister about the war. I think he was correct in expressing great concern about the war. But a statement was issued some weeks ago by the premier of Quebec to the effect that in conversation with the Prime Minister he had reached the conclusion that we were on the easy road to victory. The main part of the speech was an election manifesto of a unique and in many ways dishonest nature. It did two things. First of all it sets up the vision of a promised land knowing that the attaining of that will require machinery and constitutional changes, the former not being at present available and the latter requiring provincial agreement about which there is very great doubt. In other words, it is like giving a man a cheque for a million dollars and then telling him to go out and get somebody to sign it.
Another point about the speech from the throne is that it endorses the inflationary theme of compensation without contribution. In other words, something for nothing. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) has often and effectively used the words, "work and save", but they have now been changed to the jovial exhortation of "multiply and prosper."
At the very time the government endorses a plan of putting more purchsaing power into the hands of the people instead of providing a high and continuing degree of employment,

it brings down an order in council freezing the wages of labour in all its three categories, organized, unorganized and salaried. To aggravate matters, it uses the danger of inflation as an excuse in the very first paragraph of the order in council. Yet it brings dowm a programme which cannot by any stretch of the imagination be considered as anything but inflationary.
At the beginning of the war labour freely and wholeheartedly gave a pledge that it would not use its final and most powerful weapon, namely the strike, until the war had been won. How has labour lived up to its pledge? I believe the figures will show that during four and a half years of the war the number of man-days lost in Canada through disputes has been less on a per capita basis than those lost in any other part of the world. My own district of West York is one of the greatest industrial and railroad ridings in Canada and as far as I am aware there has not been one man-hour lost through labour disputes. This is a record of which I am extremely proud and jealous.
Now in the fifth year of the war when the problem will soon be not so much getting labour as providing employment there has been issued a highly provocative and contentious order in council known as the wartime wages control order, 1943, the provisions of which go into effect on February 15, two weeks from to-day. I should like to say a word or two about the provisions of this order which I consider to be not only provocative but completely indefensible in the light of labour's freely given pledge. The first objection is to the composition of the national labour board. I shall quote from the order in council so that the house can see what I mean. Besides the chairman and the vice-chairman, who are to be appointed by the governor in council, there are to be two other representatives of the public, then only one representing the employers and one representing the employees. With two members representing the public, who would be government appointees, there would be four members appointed by the government. The operative members, or those representing the employers' and employeees, would be outnumbered two to one, while labour would be outnumbered five to one. I think that is an entirely undue weighting of the officials on that board and that labour as well as management should receive a greater proportion of representation.
The regional boards are in a slightly different position, but the same objection applies.

The Address-Mr. Adamson
My next objection, and this is one of the most important clauses of these regulations, is that the power of the board is supreme over any court in the land. It takes precedence over any court, no matter where the court is situated and no matter what the circumstances may be. I will read the clause. The directions are final and conclusive in any court.
Any finding, direction or order given or made under the authority of this order by the national board, or by a regional board, until varied or revoked by the national board on review or appeal, shall be final and conclusive for the purpose of any proceedings in any court taken pursuant to this order and shall be accepted by and shall not be subject to review in such court.
That is a habit to which we have been accustomed through order in council. I think it is untenable and an unwise practice in this connection.
The next objectionable feature is the method of appeal from the decisions of the regional boards. This is the appeal clause:
Any person interested in or affected by any decision or direction of a regional board may appeal to the national board if the regional board making such decision or direction grants leave so to appeal.
In other words you are tried by a board and the only appeal you have from that board's decision is dependent upon the board's allowing you to appeal. That, I think, is not good legal practice, nor is it justice.
The next clause which I consider indefensible is the anti-strike clause, clause 35. It is a long clause and I shall read only a portion of it. But first let me say that after the record of labour in this dominion in this war, now in its fifth year, to bring down a clause like this which is like a red rag to a bull and would infuriate anybody is ,extremely bad policy. The clause sets out the penalties as follows:
Every employee who strikes or takes part in
any strike to obtain an increase of wages . . .
I shall not read it all, but it goes on:
.	.	. or for the purpose of obtaining any
direction from or of influencing the decision of a war labour board constituted under this order or in protest against or to obtain any alteration in any such direction . . .
Then these are the penalties:
. . . shall be guilty of an offence and liable upon summary conviction to a fine of not less than twenty-five dollars nor more than one hundred dollars or to imprisonment for a term of not less than one month nor more than three months or to both such fine and such imprisonment in respect of each day or part of a day . . .
that he is on strike.
In other words, the individual is subject to three months imprisonment for going on strike for one day or one hour. That legislation, Mr. Speaker, I contend is as restrictive and as dangerous as anything that Germany has ever had before the reichstag was abolished.
Now I come to the worst clause of all of these regulations, namely clause 36, which deals with the prosecution and the methods to be used in the prosecution. It sets out a principle that is absolutely indefensible and that is so absolutely bad that we might think we were no longer in a British country. I will read the operative part of the clause:
Where, in any prosecution of any person under this section, it is proved that such person incited, encouraged or aided any employee to go on or continue any strike the burden of proof that such strike was not in contravention of this order shall be upon the accused.

Reasonable doubt, mark you.

It is something new in British justice, something new in all our ideas of a court of law. We have taken away the right of a man to appeal. We have said that the ruling of the board takes precedence over any court and we have virtually said that the accused is guilty unless he proves he is innocent. I give the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) warning that if this goes into effect on the fifteenth of the month it will be one of the greatest causes of labour unrest that we have seen in Canada. I sincepely hope that he, in consultation with the leaders of labour, who are reasonable men, will have these provocative, indefensible and dangerous clauses amended.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that an extensive opportunity will be given for discussion of the so-called commonwealth council plan. This question cannot be dismissed after the manner of Doctor Pangloss in Candide, by saying that this is the "best of all possible worlds," after the horrible experiences we are now under-
The Address-Mr. Adamson

going. It is not perfect by any means, and to reject all suggestions for change as coming from "imperial intriguers" is to continue the petty colonial outlook which has characterized our foreign policy since the last war. As an example of this I am going to quote a paragraph with reference to something that has happened in the very recent past. I quote from'a journal known as Labotir, the journal of the American Federation of Labor and particularly of the Railroad Brotherhoods. It is discussing the world being staked out by a monopoly, the Duponts, the Imperial Chemical Company, and I. G. Farbenindustrie. The words I shall quote are not the words of a labour leader, they are not the words of an isolationist senator or member of congress. They are the words of the assistant attorney general of the United States. He is talking about monopolies and he is reported as saying:
To illustrate what he meant by dividing the world into "industrial colonies", Berge showed the effect of the cartel on Canada. He said that in order to protect the markets of the British and American companies, Canadian Industries Limited was restrained from doing any exporting or expanding. The effect, he declared, was to throttle Canadian industry and to treat Canada as a colony.
That is the present situation. We have seen in the last few weeks the closing of our greatest explosives plant. Did it have, any connection with our being treated as a colony, or did it not? These are questions which we shall have to discuss and to answer in this house.
That is all that my time will allow, but I will say this finally. I disagree with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party (Mr. Coldwell) in throwing out all discussion without adequate opportunity for this house to debate at an early date the proposals made from time to time that we as Canadians play our full part and have our voice fully heard, not only through the channels of government but through the channels of the people's representatives, first in the councils of the commonwealth and eventually in the new world order which we hope to see.

We in British Columbia are proud of the fact that during the time the present Minister of Pensions and National Health was a member of the government of that province we passed minimum wage laws. I may not get another opportunity to speak in this debate; but I should like to say that I am not always in accord with the leader of the Conservative party, yet I agree with what he said yesterday in regard to the standing army, speaking for my riding at least. Frankly we enjoy having the camp there and I must admit they are well behaved soldiers; but I tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the people of my riding can see no earthly reason for these

men being there when there is a tremendous shortage of labour in the mines and elsewhere. Mr. Speaker. I want to thank the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) for his cooperation in hurrying through his speech in order to give me an opportunity to say something before the dinner recess. I should like to take this opportunity of congratulating the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne; I think they made very excellent contributions to the debate and laid the basis for a thorough discussion of all the matters referred to in that speech. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) emphasized the necessity of getting through the business of the house as quickly as possible. I quite agree; and in my remarks this afternoon I shall be as explicit as possible in dealing with the points contained in the speech from the throne which I intend to discuss. I have no intention of dealing with all its ramifications, but before I get through I believe the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) and I may be talking to each other. That may give the minister some indication of what I intend to talk about.
In attempting, however, to hurry through the business of the house, we must not be unmindful of the fact that the speech from the throne is a very important part of that business, in that it forecasts the legislation that will be brought down. As I understand
it. any measure having to do with the affairs of Canada will be based upon the principles contained in the speech from the throne; and while we may hurry along with minor matters, I believe the measures outlined in the speech from the throne require thorough analysis by this house. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) has made a broad analysis of that speech and has touched briefly upon practically everything it contains, setting out the views of the members of this group pretty thoroughly.
At this point I should like to say that I listened with a great deal of interest to the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Roebuck), and in my opinion the discussion he carried on was timely; as a matter of fact it is long overdue. Last session the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and I put on record our opinions concerning the matters discussed this afternoon by the hon. member for Trinity, and I am heartily in accord with everything that was said by the hon. member. Without wasting time in elaborating the matter further I merely wish to place myself on record as endorsing the stand he took this afternoon in regard to the Jewish question and the part Canada should play in endeavouring to rescue what is left of these people from Hitler and those associated with him in the occupied countries.
This afternoon the hon. member for Fraser Valley and the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson) commented briefly upon the new wage order. I am not going to discuss that order at this time, but I endorse what they said in regard to the restrictions and totalitarian set-up of that legislation. Later on, when it is his turn to speak, at least one member of our group will make a thorough analysis of that order. It is a document the implications of which cannot be thoroughly discussed in the course of a fifteen or twenty minute address; but, as the hon. members pointed out, it has laid the basis for a continuing disruption of labour relations in this country which in my view may have serious repercussions in the future. As I have said, I am not going to go into the matter at this time; I merely want to place myself on record as supporting what these hon. members have said and to advise the house that hon. members of this group will continue that discussion when the opportunity arises.
In his remarks the Prime Minister made the statement that the main emphasis must continue to be on the winning of the war, and I heartily agree. While it is good policy for us to lay our plans for the future, we must not forget that the war is hot yet won

The Address-Mr. Gillis
and that there is terrific fighting ahead, with terrific sacrifices to be made by the people of this country. During the past six months I have been disturbed to find prominent men warning the people of North America, both in the press and over the air, that the war might come to a sudden end. Such propaganda is, in my opinion, designed for only one purpose, namely, to prepare the people for a negotiated peace. That is not in accordance with the policy enunciated by the united -nations, when they declared that only the unconditional surrender of the totalitarian powers will be accepted. Those who carry on the sort of propaganda that I have mentioned are doing a great disservice to the war effort of all the united nations. We must emphasize the fact that we still have to win the war. Let the people of the North American continent make no mistake about it; that is still their major task, because the termination of this war upon any terms other than the unconditional surrender of Germany and its allied powers will mean that we have lost this war and laid the basis for the next one. Nothing else can happen. In the countries of Europe that we are endeavouring to liberate there is no one but Hitler with whom to negotiate a peace, and any negotiations with him mean further appeasement and the acceptance of at least some of the ideas that he intended to foist upon the world. Therefore, in this respect I think the Prime Minister was absolutely correct when he emphasized the fact that certain opinions being expressed tend to take the minds of the people away from the real, main issue, which is the prosecution of the war to the fullest possible extent until we bring about the complete capitulation of Germany and her allies.
In my remarks this afternoon I intend to deal specifically with a most important matter which is closely related to our whole war effort and to the question of what will be the position of Canada when this war is over. In my view the two questions to which we should give the greatest consideration at this time, in an endeavour to see that the least possible disturbance is caused and the greatest possible good is done to those now in our armed services, are the matters of demobilization and reconstruction or rehabilitation. These two questions will require considerable machinery if we are to do a job on them and carry out our duty as we shall be expected to do by those now in the armed services. We must not lose sight of the fact that we in this house are privileged to talk about reconstruction and what will be the future of society on this continent, because the boys and girls in the armed forces, par-Gillis.]
ticularly those serving in theatres of war, recognized that the totalitarian military machine must be kept as far as possible from our shores and made their contribution by getting into uniform and crossing the ocean. They are there to-day. They have been successful in their mission, and have stopped the onward march of Hitler and those with whom he is associated. They are on the offensive to-day, and while the struggle may yet be severe, nevertheless they have guaranteed to us on this continent the privilege to do something about the future structure of society in Canada.
Next to the importance of winning the war, I think emphasis must be placed on the care of those who have made it possible for us to say that in the future we intend to reconstruct this country along democratic lines, and those of a Christian civilization. To them we owe the first obligation in the matter of rehabilitating Canada.
That is our first and main task. This would lead one to conclude that the government is now completely satisfied with the machinery now functioning, and that it believes such machinery is adequate to take care of this matter. I was disappointed, and I believe the government was presumptuous when it included the merchant navy in the present scheme of rehabilitation. I say that because, with the exception of extending the privilege by order in council of coming under pensions regulations for disability they are not included in the present set-up of reconstruction and rehabilitation, and must be considered as a separate unit.

In my opinion the programme is totally inadequate, and it is not working. I do not say this by way of criticism, or for the purpose of hearing myself talk or of advancing any particular political philosophy. I believe the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie), under whose department this scheme has been functioning, has been working as hard and as conscientiously as any other minister or any other member of the house. I have always found him cooperative, and quite prepared to do anything he could to adjust grievances arising from the

The Address-Mr. Gillis
regulations administered by him. I am frank, to say that about the minister. But the machinery, as it exists now, leaves much to be desired. It is my view that the machinery in the Department of Pensions and National Health is inadequate, that the department is understaffed, and cannot handle a large-scale demobilization. 1 am not satisfied, either, with the methods employed by army boards who board men out of the services and place them under the jurisdiction of the Department of Pensions and National Health. I refer to those men now returning from overseas with disabilities. I should like, however, to call to the attention of the Minister of Pensions and National Health some thoughts in connection with the administration of the Pension Act. I would remind him that in 1940 the pension committee of that year broadened the provisions of the act so that it might embrace the new forces. There was one section which had been carried for twenty-five years and which militated greatly against men who came back from the last war. I refer to the section which dealt with the men who were suffering from nervous disabilities and diseases. On seventy-five per cent of occasions, when men would appear before pension boards with disabilities of that description, the stock decision of such boards was: disability is of congenital origin, and no pension is indicated.
Hundreds of men were thrown to one side on that basis. The minister will recall that the 1940 committee removed that section from the act. I now draw to his attention the fact that while' the provision has been removed, those who are to-day administering the regulations are administering them on the old basis. He will find that a large number of men who are returning from this war-and let us remember that this is a shock-war to an even greater extent than was the last one-are suffering from nervous disabilities. When they
apply for boarding they find, in practically every instance, as shown by the decisions I have seen, that decisions are made along the same lines, namely that their disabilities are of congenital origin. The wording, of course, is a little different. At the present time the soldier is discharged and examined for pension, and if he has a disability of that description it is classified as pre-enlistment.
These men joined the services in A1 condition. They saw service in England, and have endured bombing. As a result their nerves have suffered. How can any board examining a man w7ho when he enlisted, was classed Al, and who after eighteen months in the service appears before it with a nervous condition, make the decision that the man who at the time of application is in class E, is suffering from a disability of pre-enlistment origin? The point is that this is an accusation against those who examined such men upon entering the services, and an indication that they were totally incompetent for the job they were performing. We must accept either that assumption, or the one that the boards are still administering the old section which we thought we had removed from the act. I mention these facts so that the minister may make a check with those who are boarding service personnel returning from overseas.

There is another sore spot to which I would call the attention of the minister, namely that connected with those men who are being discharged for. compassionate reasons. It may be that as a result of some extenuating circumstances at home a man may be discharged from the services. Such man, however, is not given the benefit of any of the present regulations. In fact one instance, affecting a member of the navy, was drawn to my attention. This man was discharged in Halifax and, although his home was in Vancouver, because he was discharged on compassionate grounds he was not given even his transportation expenses to his home. He had to solicit the necessary funds for that purpose. And, vice versa, I have heard of men discharged at Vancouver who have had to travel to the other side of the country.
I believe that is a wrong procedure. Such men are suffering aggravation greater than those who are coming back to normal homes. Who is more in need of Assistance than the man who comes back to a normal home?

Another grievance is in connection with the decisions that are given when men receive injuries or disabilities while serving in Canada. A man may be discharged as medically unfit; but in every case I have seen, even though the disability is admitted the decision is that the disability was incurred on service but was not attributable to military service. The two statements cannot be reconciled. I know of one case that is perhaps a little outstanding. This boy was ordered on a clothing parade and half a dozen of them got into a jeep. While they were riding along the jeep crashed into a pole. This young lad who was not driving received a fractured skull and lost the sight of one eye. He was hospitalized and discharged, but the decision was that his disability was not attributable to military service. Since that time this man has had a stroke and his case is up for another hearing. 1 do not think there should be any differentiation between the man who receives a wound overseas and the one who is injured in Canada while actually on parade. There are quite a few cases of this description.

There is another matter in the field of rehabilitation that requires overhauling. The throne speech would lead us to believe that the machinery for the placement of men discharged from the service was adequate and satisfactory. The minister will remember, as will other hon. members who were on the pension committee back in 1940, that welfare officers were to be appointed. As I understood it, these welfare officers were to look after the employment problem facing the men returning from service; they were to
[Mr. Gillis. J
work in conjunction with the officials in the unemployment insurance offices. This machinery has been partly established. J; There is one placement officer in Nova Scotia; I believe there is one in New Brunswick, and perhaps there are two in Ontario. I notice the minister is smiling. Last session he intimated he was making an appointment to the Sydney office, but that has not been made as yet. I have no doubt it will be made soon.
The number of these welfare officers should be increased. If they are to do a proper job there should be one welfare officer in every unemployment insurance office. This is necessary in order that the preference which has been delegated to those who return from overseas or from the service in Canada is carried out. If we are not to have proper machinery there is no use in doing anything about it. The machinery we have to-day is totally inadequate.
The work of these placement officers was to be supplemented by the appointment of citizen committees in every section. These committees w-ere to supplement the work of the placement officers in probing fields of employment for those men who are coming back. Little was done about .this until November of last year when a committee was convened to consist of the mayors of some of the towns and cities across Canada.
' These volunteer committees are to return to their respective communities and endeavour to take care of the employment needs of the men who return from the services. That machinery is not going to work. These committees are not responsible to anyone. They have no machinery with which to work; they have no offices and they have no authority to do anything for anyone. I think it is a complete waste of time to expect volunteer citizen committees throughout the country to take care of this question of demobilization and rehabilitation. This machinery might have worked a year ago when there were just a few dribbling back, but I visualize the time when there will be total demobilization of alt the service personnel. I think the time has arrived when we should have the proper machinery and the proper administrative authority which would be responsible to some department of government.
I think the suggestion in the speech from the throne that three new departments are to be set up is a good one, and these questions of reestablishment and rehabilitation should be centred in one of these departments. In my opinion this idea of citizen committees should be forgotten and immediate steps taken to increase the number of welfare officers in order

The Address-Mr. Gillis
to have one in ever}- unemployment insurance office. It would be their duty to find available employment and to see that preference is given to the ex-service men. They should provide advice and guidance in the whole field of rehabilitation. They would have the proper places in which to work and would be responsible to some one. There must be sufficient personnel to handle this problem. Under the present set-up the ex-service man is coming back and is being routed through the regular employment offices. This will continue if the present economic set-up as visualized by the people in power to-day is carried into effect. In addition to the men coming back from the services there will be a million war workers. The present machinery is totally inadequate and does not differentiate between those who have a preference and those to whom no preference has been given.
There is another point in connection with the rehabilitation of veterans to which I should like to refer. Some provision has been made for vocational training and guidance for those coming out of the service who have sufficient elementary education to fit themselves into the present scheme, but there are hundreds or perhaps thousands of boys coming back who have not the degree of education to enable them to take advantage of the present vocational training schemes. I have run into quite a number of them. These men are discharged as medically unfit and they apply to the selective services offices for a job. They write to Halifax to Colonel MacKenzie for a rehabilitation grant or vocational training, but word comes back that nothing can be done about vocational training. Many of these boys have never had jobs and that is the situation they find themselves in to-day. I think there is adequate machinery in the country and it should be used, and used immediately, to do something for this category of ex-service men. I refer to the schools that are now operating. One is in North Bay, and there are three others where illiterate personnel in the service are given an elementary education. The schools are working efficiently and have a very good system. I had the privilege of going through the school at North Bay, and I highly commend it. I think that branch of our educational work should be not only continued but expanded, in order to give this class of boy an opportunity to reestablish himself as a useful member of society. Without such an opportunity he is in the middle of the street; there is no prospect for him. nothing for him to do, and certainly the developing situation with respect to employment leaves much to be desired so far as he is concerned. I leave those thoughts with the minister.
It is not possible for me to tell the whole story, Mr. Speaker, in forty minutes. I have been trying to provoke the minister's thought. I have a lot more to say but my time is limited.
I should like to say a word or two with respect to the machinery of demobilization. That matter will have to be considered. We owe it to the boys who are overseas at the present time and who have been there, some of them, for a long period, to consider what is going to happen on demobilization. There is no doubt that we shall have an army of occupation when the war is over. If that is the case, I think service in such an army should be on a voluntary basis and that reinforcements for that army should be on a voluntary basis. Furthermore, we may have to maintain a large standing army, navy and air force to meet our international obligations in the field, of world peace. I think the first choice to serve in such an army, navy and air force, to man and operate it, should go to those who are now serving in an actual theatre of war. Those who are serving at home, while they are making a valuable contribution, have not suffered as have those who have been in actual combat with the enemy. Those who are in service at home are in a position to keep their finger on everything worth-while in the country, and if anything develops which means a future for them they have the opportunity to get there first. But those who are serving overseas have not that opportunity, and so I would like those who have served overseas in an actual theatre of war to be given the first choice to serve in such a force. The Canadian government should insist that our army of occupation retain its Canadian identity and be manned by Canadians, with Canadian officers to look after those of our boys who may desire to serve in that army.
As regards the matter of discharge, undoubtedly considerable machinery will be necessary. We should not do what was done in the last war. Then, when we came back from Europe, we were split up into different camps. Personally I was with a Vancouver unit when the wind-up came. We were taken back to England and shipped to demobilization camps in north Wales. It was not a very nice place to be. But they closed our pay books there, and we were fed very poorly.
I think it should be the policy of the Canadian government as soon as hostilities cease to bring our boys back from Europe as soon as possible; that is, those who want to come back, and the procedure of demobilization should be gone through in Canada. I think the camps we now have all across the

The Address-Mr. Gillis
country are adequate for that purpose. Once the men are back in Canada they should be sent to their respective military districts for demobilization.
But before demobilization or discharge there is one thing we should do. Every man in the service on coming back to Canada should be given a month's furlough to allow him to go home and look over employment conditions in his own part of the country. That would enable him to make up his mind where he would like to go. After the last war the men were permitted to take their discharge in any part of Canada or the United States. But we should remember that the employment situation is going to be complicated after this war and we should see to it that every man who comes back has the training necessary to fit him into the employment picture so that he may be able to make his best contribution. In that connection vocational training is very important, and I leave the thought with the minister that we have machinery now functioning in Canada which could be used effectively just by reversing the present process. I mean that we have army personnel or induction boards which consider the aptitudes of a man who is entering the service and route him into the branch where he can make his best contribution. The personnel in charge of this work has been trained for four years and has cost a considerable sum of money. It is doing good service, I am informed, and if it can route men who are entering the service into the branch where they can render the best contribution, then it seems reasonable that, on demobilization, it could route the men who are leaving the service into gainful occupation or into opportunities where their services can best be used. That would merely be a reversing of the present machinery.
The schools now operating, army, navy and air force, should also be fully utilized, as well as the schools set up by industry. All these schools should be expanded, if necessary. The Canadian Legion's war services educational personnel which has been largely absorbed by the defence organizations, should also be fully utilized, because they have a highly trained personnel whose services should be taken advantage of. We should not be political about the thing at all but see that that machinery is used to the best advantage in the period of demobilization and rehabilitation.
It is almost six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, and my time is about up. I have much more to say. but I shall reserve it for another occasion.

I am more convinced than ever to-day that had such a minister been appointed, a great deal of the waste that has taken place in connection with foodstuffs during the past year would have been avoided. During the war years there has been a tremendous increase in hog production on the prairies where the same producers grow the feed and finish the hogs on the same farms. In 1943, Alberta had not only the highest swine population in the history of the province, some 2,337,700 hogs, but the highest ever recorded by any province in the Dominion of Canada. This was quite a record and I think it is something which we had been advised to do over a period of years. We were told that the grain should be marketed through the live stock. These farmers are to be congratulated upon the advance they had made in this respect. Then in the midst of that we had this announcement from the government which completely demoralized all their plans. It was certainly unhealthy and something which I think should have been prevented had we a properly organized food ministry in this country. While they have accomplished that fine record in Alberta the province stood very high in the dominion in the percentage of man-power and woman-power contributed to the armed forces of Canada. It was one of the leading provinces and I think it speaks highly for Alberta and for the other prairie provinces.
Following the government's announcement on Canada's decreased hog production for 1944, the Right Hon. Colonel J. J. Llewellin, Minister of Food for Great Britain, arrived on the scene and somewhat straightened out

On, account of very abnormal weather early this winter there was a very large egg production in this country, when the authorities set the present' prices of eggs, and as a result many poultry producers have already changed their plans for 1944 production, because the return, for eggs is out of line with the cost of feeds and labour. While we have an immense egg production today there will be a decrease rather than an increase a year hence as a result of these prices.
Butter fat with bonus is approximately forty-four cents a pound in Canada. Butter fat with subsidy is approximately 54-9 cents a pound in the. United States. Much has been said in past debates in this house about the Canadian farmer's share of the national income. For the period 1926 to 1940, 74 -2 per cent of the national income went to the workers and to the farmers of Canada. Labour constituted five-twelfths of the population and received 62-4 per cent of the national income; the farmers constituted four-twelfths of the population and received 11-8 per cent of the national income. That is what they received for their work and their capital investment, which is considerable. There is some disparity there. The average monthly farm wage for the three prairie provinces has increased during the war from $30.13 to $61.17, and the harvest daily wage from $2.86 to $5.56. To be on a par with organized labour it should be further increased, as I pointed out to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell), the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) in the debates on April 2, 1943, which may be found on pages 1808-9, and on May 20, 1943 at pages 2928-9. I believe that farm labour should be guaranteed the same basis of remuneration, as organized labour in this country, but there is a great disparity.

It seems to me if there is any meaning to this new order we have had placed before us in very vague terms in the speech from the throne, this insurance principle shotdd be made applicable to all members of the armed forces who are on active service anywhere.
I was disappointed this afternoon when a committeee was set up to deal with the election act and the taking of the votes of the soldiers overseas. I do think the terms of the reference should have been made broader, and at a time like this our election act should have been overhauled. Personally I think we should have the transferable vote for single member constituencies. Hon. members may not realize that of the 245 members of this house seventy-four are here by virtue of having received a minority vote in their constituencies. In a democratic nation, which we think is progressive, it is certainly time to correct that situation. I am the more surprised that nothing has been done in this regard because of the fact that in the chart or guide mentioned by the Prime Minister, which he brought forth in 1919, something of this kind was advocated. Surely at this time we should overhaul the election act and make provision for the transferable vote in single member constituencies. Mr. Speaker, we have in this house an official whose loyal sendees merit the attention of parliament; a doctor of law, a king's counsel, a member of the Royal Society of Canada, who has been Clerk of the House of Commons for almost twenty years. Doctor Beauchesne recently published the third edition of his "Parliamentary Rules and Forms," the work of a master, covering almost nine hundred pages. This wonderful work was prepared by the author primarily for the use of members of this house, and I wish to extend to him my deep gratitude and satisfaction, and to express the sincere hope that the French translation of this most useful work will be made available without delay. Both languages are official in Canada, and we are only claiming our right when we ask for. this translation.
The programme for the present session denotes the anxiety of the government in the face of the serious problems which exist in this country. Never since 1935 has the speech from the throne been of such an election character. Who does not recall the anxiety of the Bennett government, which was in power at that time? The Prime Minister of that time sought, by a supreme effort of social legislation, to remedy what was impossible to remedy. He had gained power by virtue of so many promises. The government which followed, was satisfied with denying its formal commitments while asserting candidly that it could not keep them any more. It even asked its voters to forget about its pledges and heaven knows under what circumstances and

through what means. This was done by obtaining the monopoly of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in spite of the most elementary justice. The head of a certain party is now complaining about the C.B.C. Why did he not do so when the plebiscite was held? The leaders of the four main political parties in Canada then tolerated the most shameful dictatorship, which gagged thousands of citizens. Through their action they were responsible for making the fight unjust and unequal in favour of the "yes" and against the "no."
As regards the social legislation introduced by the government, history repeats itself with this difference, that the former government made its calculations in peace time while this government adds, subtracts and divides in war time.
The government says that the first of its ends is to win the war. The second is to face post-war conditions. In order to attain this end, it must do better than move a whole complexity of social legislation. In order to win the peace, it must remedy the social upheavals which it has caused. Four hundred thousand men have abandoned their farms. More than 100,000 women also have abandoned the land in spite of the numerous warnings given by our best economists. The government is doing even worse. It insists upon calling back for a revision of their medical examinations the young farmers, who must fill out the new forms in order to obtain a new postponement. This is a loss of time, and a source of annoyance and bother for the agricultural class which, more than ever, needs all its help and all its time.
The sessional programme refers to a price ceiling on agricultural products. Why not set a price ceiling on foodstuffs which are sold by trusts at prohibitive prices. Wholesale prices of milling by-products per carload and per ton: Barley flour from $38 to $40, and crushed oats from $42 to $44.25 on the Montreal and Quebec markets.

More than a billion dollars was spent in direct relief. No money could be found for public works, no salaries for labourers, no work for our sons and daughters. The treasury was empty, for constructive works. But on account of the participation of Canada in this war the government suddenly discovered $10,000,000000, and more, for destructive work. He is turned down because, owing to his health, this man cannot be recommended for another employment by the selective service. If he were refunded the amount of the dues which he paid, he could support his wife and his three children. The figures given in the January, 1944, issue of Canada at War confirm these striking facts.
