Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. ' To me as a newcomer they
were symbolic of the growing national unity, a unity between English and French-speaking Canada. They were symbolic of Canada at war; for as soldiers they expressed the sentiments of the armed forces and their relation to the problems of the home front.
I am especially appreciative of the remarks made by the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) regarding the participation in the war of men hailing from new Canadian stock. It is a better understanding between the national groups of Canada, between peoples of all races and religions who make up the population of our country, that will lead to a strong and democratic Canada.
Likewise, in our international relations it is the conviction of our party that the Teheran, Moscow and Cairo conferences have laid the basis of a great new epoch of human developments. I quote from the declaration of the Teheran conference:
We express our determination that our nations shall work together in the war and in the peace that will follow. As to the war, our military staffs have joined in our roundtable discussions and we have concerted our plans for the destruction of the German forces. And as to the peace, we are sure that our concord will make it an enduring peace. We recognize fully the supreme responsibility resting upon us and all the nations to make a peace which will command good-will from the overwhelming masses of the peoples of the world and banish the scourge and the terror of war for many generations. . . . We shall seek the cooperation andi active participation of all nations, large and small, whose peoples in heart aud mind are dedicated, as are our own people, to the elimination of tyranny and slavery, oppression and intolerance. We look with confidence to the day when all the peoples of the world may live free lives untouched by tyranny, according to their varying desires and their own consciences.
Here we have a great charter for victory and a better world, not only a charter based on the big powers, as some tend to interpret the Teheran conference declaration, but for all peoples large and small, a charter which shall become the rallying point on a national and international scale.
Before the Moscow, Teheran and Cairo conferences there were danger signs which led many to start speaking about "world war No. 3". There was loose talk about Anglo-Saxon powers running the world. Appeasement raised its head in the form of Darlans, Peyroutons, and similar hirelings in Italy, Yugoslavia, Greece and Austria. An attempt was made to force upon the peoples of Europe the type of leaders who had ruled on behalf of wealthy cliques and had sold their people down the river. The heroic people of China were given all sorts of sympathy and very little else. In fact, in certain of the united
The Address-Mr. Rose

nations circles it was considered indiscreet to attack the emperor of Japan. To-day, following the conferences, there is a vision of free peoples who are fighting to reestablish democratic rule and who, although hesitantly, are getting some help from the leading powers within the united nations. We see the world war becoming one of national liberation. A good example (5f this we see in Yugoslavia, where, instead of a country run by the Serbs, all of the nationalities on an equal basis and with equal opportunities are fighting heroically and winning world recognition. They have established a national assembly of their own.
This is the new age which we see coming into the world at the present time, although with difficulty. The Italian people are, through the Italian commission, gradually winning some possibility to join with the peoples of the united nations in fighting against the nazi murderers for the establishment of a democratic regime, purged of those elements that have dragged their country down to their present difficult condition. In the far east, a free China will be a powerful force for world peace and will go a long way in influencing and securing freedom for hundreds of millions of Hindus, Burmese and other peoples.
As for Canada, I want to emphasize that our own prosperity, freedom, peace and security depend upon a world living under similar circumstances. If one needed any proof of the truth of this, we saw it in the case of the present war. No amount of isolationism could have left us undisturbed.
We have contributed very substantially towards Hitler's plight at the present time. But, as stated in the speech from the throne, "the German army is still very strong." The hardest battles are still coming; and our job is to have an eye on the ball, the battles against the nazis and the Japanese, rather than to fight for parties and advantage. In the face of this test of strength before which we stand, the measure of national unity which we have had in the past should be continued for the duration of the war and for the immediate post-war period.
Unless we are able to preserve national unity, we shall, in our petty quibbling, let down our boys in the armed forces and bring them back after victory is ours into a state of unrest and chaos. I appeal to all parties to work in this spirit of comradeship. That is the spirit of our heroic men in the services, the men of the merchant marine who deliver the goods, the hundreds of thousands of war workers, men and women, who spare no effort to see that we have the goods to deliver. I appeal
(Mr Rose.]
to all parties to unite in combatting the forces that would rob us of democratic progress in a free world.
Voices are raised by certain individuals, one of whom the horn, member for Dorchester rightly characterized as "le tapa-geur". These are voices that I would call the voices of inhumanity. We have just had a veiy fine example of it in the previous speaker, the hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains (Mr. Lacombe). These people, consciously or unconsciously, do the work of the enemy, who in the face of certain defeat, tries to resort to the old worn-out bogey of bolshevism to split the united nations. They take up every argument from the enemy's baggage. Irresponsibly they speak of the impossibility of international unity. They say it will not last; it cannot last; Russia will betray us. And certain scribes of the newspapers use their poison pens to slander the soviet people, whose glorious efforts mean so much to every one of us, to every one of our families. Indeed, many of us would not be here if it were not for their heroic efforts. In the nazi manner they concoct plots and talk about a hundred thousand Jewish refugees who are going to chase the French-Canadian farmers off their land. They discover plots of international Jewry, but Jewry is not the only one who plots. There is freemasonry, and when you say that "free" you want to emphasize it. They resort very openly to Hitler's weapon of antiSemitism. These elements, although small, are a threat to national and international unity. They are a threat to Canada and Canada's well-being.
Another group are unprincipled enough to resort to any trickery to defeat the desire of our people for a better Canada and a better world. They are the elements who have raised the bogey of socialism and confiscation of savings, and I would not be a bit surprised if in the very near future they said that the socialists were out to nationalize women.
Mr. Speaker, the issue to-day is not what these people call free enterprise versus socialism ; the issue is democratic progress versus chaos and insecurity. Our party, the Labour Progressive party, stands for socialism, but we are realistic enough to know and to understand that the vast majority of Canadians are to-day not yet ready for it. We consider that at this time the fight for social progress is a fight in which the people will learn, through their own experience, whether or not they want socialism. The essence of socialism is democracy, and it will not come until the majority of Canadians learn through their experience that socialism is the system they need.

The Address-Mr. Rose
It is in this spirit that I welcome the promises of far-reaching reforms contained in the speech from the throne. Without such reforms, and others which have been omitted, we cannot hope to have national unity. The promise of family allowances is good. 1 am not surprised to find people who have been talking about family allowances taking the attitude today, not exactly that they oppose such allowances, but that they are not so good. Well, I do not believe that the people in Quebec will fall for any such talk. They will accept family allowances no matter what party introduces the principle. They will be glad to have it. But family allowances must not replace measures for increased wages for labour. Family allow'ances must not become a bonus to employers, but must be a few extra dollars to people whereby they can buy more milk and more nutrition for their families.
I also believe that family allowances should not be limited to four, five or six children. I do not know how many it is to be, but if it is good for six children, what 'will the seventh, the eighth and the ninth do? And in our province there are large families. It is unjust to stop at five or six. The issue of family allowances should not be raised as against improving wages. When I speak of wages I think of those paid in our province which are still very low in comparison with those paid in other provinces. I have in mind the thousands of textile workers. For the past year they have been carrying on a just fight to get increased wages. Some of them earn wages as low as 22 cents an hour, and family allowances must not stand in the way of these people getting a just increase in wages. Something has to be done about these textile workers in our province. They have been patient-so much so that one member of the house said to me: "Je pense qu'il y a quelque chose qui ne marche pas dans cette union"; "there is something wrong with the union." There is nothing wrong with the union, if they do not want to bring workers out on strike at the present time. They could 'have done it. Would that have been just? Would that have been the way for them to get increases? If the federal government has not the power to deal with this key problem to national unity, what confidence can the people have in the power of the government to apply other measures mentioned in the speech from the throne? I have been told,
I may be wrong, that the Premier of Quebec suddenly became what we call provincial autonomy conscious in regard to labour problems and rushed to introduce a bill in Quebec which has won the condemnation of labour forces in the city of Montreal and the province of Quebec. I believe the people of my province will approve measures that will result in improvements in their welfare. Too often have autonomous rights been used by unscrupulous politicians to keep the people of our province in a state of inequality. No doubt the same constitutional objections could be raised in connection with the housing problem. I know that this constitutional problem exists; but again, what are we to do? We have a catastrophic housing problem in the city of Montreal. I am going to quote to the house letters I have received. Some five thousand people may be out of their homes by May 1, 1944. As hon. members know, under order 294 a family can be told to get out of their home if somebody has enough money and makes sufficient profit to buy that home. That home can be taken from them on six months' notice. Where is that family to go? I say it is a criminal act against the war effort. I have received all sorts of letters from people and have had many people come to visit me. Before I cite the cases I should state that there has been an amendment to order 294 whereby only the person who buys the home can force the occupants out of it within six months. In Montreal about five thousand families will be without homes unless we do something about the matter.

Here is a man with a family of five; he has one son in the navy and another one in the army overseas. They have nowhere to go. I shall read

(Text): They have tried to take houses and change them into apartments. plan to include such things as the development of the St. Lawrence waterway, the development of our vast hydro electric power resources, rural electrification, the development of our natural resources, the modernization and reconstruction of our cities, the abolition of slums, the rebuilding of libraries and hospitals, and the development of modern highways to give our people work. We are an important country from the point of view of production, but what very often happens? We get the orders; we are assigned something; we are just a small contractor, though we have a large production. Look at the United States; through lend-lease they have helped a number of countries, but they have also advertised American goods. Where do we stand? I believe that the aid we grant should be given more directly to the countries involved. We must win their good will to-day for trade to-morrow, for we shall need plenty of trade if we are to give work to everyone. We might increase trade through long term credits to the people of Europe, and let me repeat that we can stake out our share of that trade to-day by dealing with those countries directly rather than indirectly. We are a sovereign nation; let us act as one.
I understand that we are playing quite an important role in the operations of the united nations relief and rehabilitation organization. We are going to supply quite a large amount of material in that connection; in fact if I am not mistaken the head of that commission is a Canadian. I believe they should attend to the war and leave the rehabilitation authorities to handle rehabilitation matters. Then we shoqld let the people know who gives them the goods they receive in their time of need. Yes, we have shown in time of war that we are an important country; we have proved that we can make an important contribution to the world, and we must continue to do so in time of peace, but we must be united and we must be strong.
In this connection I should like to refer to an issue which is being used too often in Canada to divide our people; that is, the issue of anti-Semitism, the issue of racial discrimination, which was used by Hitler to make barbarians' out of decent human beings. We have quite a lot of that in Canada. There is no use in adopting a hush-hush policy; I do not believe in it. Recently I have seen some literature which has been distributed in Quebec w'hich is a disgrace to a civilized nation. Jews are painted almost as people with horns, and this literature is being distributed throughout the countryside, where some people have never seen a Jew, so they may actually believe that they are exactly as this literature says. I have had negroes come to me and ask, "Why cannot we get into that dance hall? Why cannot we get jobs? Why do we have it so hard in the air force or the army?" We have the amti-Catholic agitation being carried on by certain people in Ontario. I say that for the sake of unity in Canada the time has come when a royal commission should be set up to investigate all these anti-Canadian activities which are splitting us asunder when we should be strongly united.
I now come to the end of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, which I believe have been made in the spirit in which the Labour-Progressive party wants to work; that is, in the desire to contribute toward a democratic and prosperous Canada. Sometimes I think that certain parties should forget the idea that- they have a monopoly on contributions of this kind. We all have a contribution to make for the sake of Canada, for the people of Canada and toward a united effort. So let us go forward to build the type of world that was foreseen by our great leaders when they met in Teheran not so long ago.

Mr. Speaker, may I first of all, congratulate the mover and the seconder of the address in reply, upon the eloquent way in which they performed their difficult task. I should like also, if I may, to extend a welcome to the new member for Cartier, Montreal (Mr. Rose), who has just taken his seat. He has expressed himself very clearly, and I hope he will continue to contribute something worth while to the good work of this assembly.
The war has been going on for a long time, and I wish at the outset of my remarks to pay tribute to the record of the government in handling our war effort. This has been mentioned in editorials of many publications, and people from coast to coast are realizing that those who are guiding and directing the efforts of the Canadian people are doing a splendid job, and are deserving

The Address-Mr. Gershaw

of recognition and credit. Standing close to where you now sit, Mr. Speaker, Madame Chiang Kai-shek said that Canada had contributed more per capita to the war effort than any other of the allied countries. Credit for this is due to the patriotism and the enthusiastic response of thousands of Canadian men and women who have set aside their own affairs, and rallied to the service of their country. All honour to those who have courageously joined the armed forces, or spent long hours labouring in industrial plants! All honour to those who have continued to produce the food supplies of this country! Often they have been poorly paid for so doing. Often they have worked at tasks almost beyond their physical ability. And let us never forget the contribution the women have made in so many different capacities, often working long hours in their homes, providing comforts for the soldiers.
The contribution the people of Canada, working as a united nation, have made to the war effort has amazed the world. Let us look at some of the departments of government. The navy, starting with fifteen ships, and some 1,774 men, has expanded until it now has more than 600 ships and more than 70,000 men and officers. An English magazine, Shipping, says that this is an all-time record; it has never been excelled. That navy has patrolled and guarded our shores. Its ships have sailed the seven seas, side by side with the vessels of the British fleet. They have convoyed forty-seven per cent of the material crossing the Atlantic to the united nations.
A United States publication says that if these convoys had not been kept running the allies would have lost the war. A vast Canadian army has been organized.. Thousands of airmen have been trained. Those airmen fly four, five or six miles into the thin, cold air. Their efforts are hampered by sleet, clouds and storms. They are harassed by enemy action. They are performing deeds almost beyond human endurance. Indeed, they are making a mighty contribution to the destruction of Hitler.
Then, in connection with the Department of Munitions and Supply, Mr. Churchill when speaking in the United States referred to our output as Canada's massive production. The holding of the price ceiling has been one of the most difficult and, politically, most costly, tasks in so far as the present government is concerned. The New York Times recently said that against war-time inflation Canada's defences have been the best of any of the allied nations. These things have required thought and planning, and it is not by accident that the stores in Canada contain nearly

all commodities that are required. It is not by accident that the Canadian dollar retains about four-fifths of its pre-war purchasing power.
Mistakes have been made, and before taking my seat I shall enumerate some of them. Legislation, which has proven to be good, and will stand as a monument to those who have put it on the statute books, has been passed. I shall refer to some of that legislation. But there are still great problems to be faced, and great dangers and difficulties ahead. This is no time for complacency. This generation must move, not backward but forward, to greater economic and political freedom. All are now agreed that a mistake was made during the ten long years of depression when, in Canada and in other countries, many people were unemployed and were on the breadlines. All are determined that this condition of affairs shall never arise again, and ex-service men, particularly, will never endure or permit the recurrence of such a condition of affairs.
To prevent a return of those days of depression, reconstruction committees under the direction of hon. members have been planning to bring about a condition under which there will be full employment, so far as it is humanly possible to arrange it. There has been planning to revive the coal industry in the little provinces down by the sea, to reclaim land in the central provinces, irrigating the dry prairies wherever it is possible to do so. There is planning for shipbuilding and the development of fisheries of the coastal provinces. Everywhere in Canada roads, schools, hospitals and bridges will be built, and particular attention has been paid to the building of homes in rural and urban districts.	-
There is one other problem which must be faced-and this I wish to emphasize as my chief object in speaking to-night-namely that agriculture must be put on a paying basis. Anyone going into the homes of average western farmers will realize that the returns in that industry are not as good as those in other industries. People on the farms plan for better buildings and better conditions. They entertain the hope that their children can be educated, so that they may enjoy a better life. But dreams on the farms seldom come true, because of the many hazards which must be faced. If we took man-hours, woman-hours and child-hours required to produce agricultural products we would find that their values are not comparable with values in other industries. It is quite true that at the present time statistics may show that farmers have more money than they have ever had. But they are frustrated, and they have been

exasperated by the many seemingly needless orders which are issued. An order in council will come out which is difficult to understand; it will be long and confusing. Then an amendment will come out and a short time later the order in council may be cancelled. This is all most confusing.
Recently we heard of a bonus on oats and barley. The first announcement was received with consternation in the feeding districts. Later on, the order in council was explained and then a few weeks later a further explanation was issued. In the district whence I come there was a complete crop failure in 1943; even the grass did not grow. In order to meet a condition of this kind I would once more bring to the attention of the house the necessity of irrigating these dry areas. They have a maximum amount of sunshine, the soil is fertile, the only thing required is water. I want to thank the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) for sending out engineers to compile complete records on the engineering phase of one irrigation scheme in southern Alberta. When the war ends it is expected that there will be some measure of employment, and it is to be hoped that these projects will have reached a stage where tenders can be called for and the work started at once. If that is done it will provide homes for those who have been faced with failure or perhaps for those who are returning from the war. It will provide traffic for our railways and provide work for the building trades, for our coal miners and for live stock feeders.
We all want to live as long as we can and we all want to enjoy as much health as we possibly can. Nutritionists tell us that the foods that we generally lack are dairy products and fruits and vegetables. These are the products of irrigated districts. By the development of these districts and the putting in of quick freezing plants these products would be available all year. This would be a great blessing to those who live in parts of the country where such products are difficult to obtain. There are some cooperative processing plants in the district, but there is a danger of their being put out of business. They are not government inspected and thus they do not qualify for the bonus which is being paid for hogs at the present time. This is not fair.

I should like to refer to some of the legislation which I believe is working out well and which will prove to be a credit to the members of this deliberative assembly. In. May, 1941, when payrolls were good and when many people were employed the unemployment insurance scheme was placed upon our statute books. The workers now have an equity of $180,000,000 -in that fund. Employers, employees and the government all contribute. An employee receiving 120 a week pays thirty cents a week. If he has worked five years and becomes unemployed he can receive $10.20 a week if he is single or $12 a week if he is married for a period of fifty-two weeks. The government is paying the dues of the men in the armed services. If they go into an included occupation -when they return they will find themselves in good standing.
As I mentioned when an amendment was being considered last session, it is unfortunate that invalidity and sickness insurance was not included in the Unemployment Insurance Act. The workmen's compensation boards in the provinces look after accident cases, but those who are sick, those who are disabled by any means other than accident find it very difficult when a calamity of this kind overtakes them. Wages, salaries and profits in this country are not sufficient to enable anyone to meet these hazards. I do hope that this problem will be considered under unemployment insurance.
Because of the action of the Alberta government and the dominion government, pioneers in Alberta who are over seventy years of age may now get $30 a month from some source. This problem of old age pensions is mentioned in the speech from the throne and I do hope that something more will be done. I contend that casual earnings should be allowed to reach a higher figure than is allowed at the present time. The years that go by take a toll from the human system and whether we will admit it or not, age creeps up upon us all. When a person reaches the age of sixty-five years he is no longer able to do strenuous work, and so I hope that legislation will be placed upon our statute books to give some relief to those who have readhed the age of sixty-five years and are able to qualify otherwise.
A short time ago a dominion inheritance tax was imposed. Wealthy estates are taxed heavjly, but the tax is light on the smaller estates. Those below $5,000 are exempt altogether; a widow is exempt up to $20,000, and each child up to $5,000. Near relatives get more out of an estate than do distant relatives. We impose an income tax up to ninety or ninety-two per cent on large incomes, but we have made the burden light on those who are least able to pay. Our income tax is lower

on the lower incomes and higher on the higher incomes than is the tax in either the United States or Great Britain. For example, a man earning $700 in Canada pays $13; in the United States he would have to pay $40. and in Great Britain, $45. But if a man has an income of $30,000, in Canada he would have to pay $18,396; in the United States $13,761 and in Great Britain, $18,217.
Vocational training in this country has been a great success. Thousands of young men have been taught trades and have proved to be very useful during this war. They will be most useful after the termination of the war. Vocational braining is being planned for those who return from service overseas. During the last war this type of training was available only for minors and those who were injured during the war, but now it is available for all who can benefit by it, men and women alike. During the time these people are taking training, or when they are convalescent or out of work, they are paid an allowance. A single man can get $10.20 a week, while the married man with children will get a higher rate. The married man with four children can get $24 a week. In Australia and New Zealand these rates are slightly lower and they are paid for only thirteen weeks, whereas in Canada payments may be made for fifty-two weeks, and in cases where education is being continued, for as long as four years.
Thousands of contracts are awarded every week for guns, tanks, ships, planes, motor vehicles, et cetera. There is no preferred or patronage list in connection with these contracts. Anyone, everyone, is allowed to tender; and precautions are taken which show that care is being exercised in the handling of these contracts. For instance, every contract for over $2,000 has to be approved by the head of the branch; every contract or agreement over $5,000 by the deputy minister, and every contract over $15,000 by the cabinet. In addition to that there is a purchase investigating committee. This is a group of business men who go into every contract and every agreement to see that there are no weaknesses and no favouritism. In addition, cost accountants check all agreements and contracts and they are responsible to the auditor general. Also we have a parliamentary committee on war expenditure that may dip into any one of these contracts.
Canada has taken a leading part in international conventions, at Hot Springs and other places, looking to a freer exchange of goods, and with the purpose of feeding the starving people of Europe when they are liberated
fMr. Gershaw.]
from the heel of the oppressor. Already half the people of Greece are living on Canadian wheat.
The average Canadian, Mr. Speaker, does not want to embark on vague experiments. He wants victory to come as soon as possible. He wants to be assured of a decent standard of living when victory is won. He *wants this war to bring a lasting peace. Toward those objectives we in Canada must keep driving with all the courage and fortitude that we can muster, if we would have that future wherein our childreen can walk in ways of peace and happiness. Truly a glorious opportunity lies before our people; they can rise to heights to which they have never before attained. As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) has said, "if we in this country keep our heads and pursue high objectives, we shall achieve results in the post-war world which will amaze civilization."

Mr. Speaker, the framers of the speech from the throne which is now being debated have missed their vocation. They should have followed the vocation of window-dressing, because the speech is the most expert piece of windowdressing which I have seen in this parliament.
The main matter before the country to-day is, what is to become of Canada and the British empire after the war Yet there is no eut-and-dried foreign policy, nor is there an announcement of any empire policy at all.
In referring to the speech from the throne the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) referred yesterday to various imperial conferences which have been held, in 1926, 1937 and other years, when Canada took the position that we had no commitments but that parliament would decide. But parliament did not decide anything except to enter the war ten days late.
It seems to me that the issue in this debate is not one of Canada's autonomy, her status, or her sovereignty. There is no intention on the part of the mother of parliament to interfere with any of these things. Some of those who have spoken thus far seem to have searched Old Mother Hubbard's cupboard for skeletons of the past, and dragged into this debate a great many things which should have been forgotten long ago, and should not be resurrected, if we are to win this war, at a time when unity is so badly needed. The war is primary; nothing else matters now. The domestic questions which this country has to deal with, although they are of great importance, can be deferred until we know whether we are going to win this war and whether we are going to have collective security or not. The position

The Address-Mr. Church
of the Prime Minister is not altogether consistent with the policy in which, I am convinced, all the people of Canada of all parties believe, in what he said was primary, namely the winning of the war. What is the object of going through two world wars like these in a little over twenty years when we shall have the very same condition of affairs again unless the dominions are united with the mother country in the post-war world to come? Britain cannot exist without the dominions. Her very life is at stake; she has to import twenty-five out of twenty-seven raw materials, and she is dependent upon the dominions. Unless they are a unit in their foreign policy and empire policy, the outlook for the empire and for the mother country is very dark. The dominions must hang together or they will hang separately, because none of the dominions is able ta "go it" alone. Together they are the greatest in the world. We have seen what has happened to the small states in Europe; they have been overrun by the mechanized hordes of the German and other dictators.
One of the great prime ministers of France said a few years ago that Britain was the hardest country in the world to make a treaty with; she always spoke with so many voices. With Canada's present sovereign status, hardly a day goes by that some ambassador is'1 not sent out to this or that country, all over the seven seas. These people used to be called ministers or envoys extraordinary, and a great many of them were extraordinary. In the twenty years between the two -wars we created a number of ministers plenipotentiary. Now as full ambassadors they have brand new uniforms -at the country's expense, if you please-and there are so many of them that the government has a hard time to find anybody left in Canada to take the job. Dear knows who the next one will be or where he will be sent. This is one phase and one consequence of the policy of isolationism and separatism which Canada has pursued.
The right policy for this country was laid down by the Progressive Conservative party, and they have adhered to it since 1844. It is a consistent empire and foreign affairs policy. Some people are talking about "British imperialism." The word "imperialism" is a misnomer. It is used by the same people who in the period betrveen the two wars forgot all about German imperialism, opposed rearmament, and thought we could depend for peace and security on Geneva. It is the humbug of Geneva which -was largely responsible for this second war. We in Canada owe everything we have to the mother country. For two years after 1939 she went it all alone with the help of the dominions, standing
against the dictators of the world, and we here, the people of Quebec especially, owe her a great deal. Had the enemy sailed up the St. Lawrence with his land, air and sea forces we would have had no defence at all. Yet there are some who wanted to reduce our military estimates to one dollar-some who are now going through the country posing as super-patriots and criticizing "British imperialism." They never said one word about German and Japanese and Italian imperialism, and the menace of it before this war, as they preached pacifism and disarmament.
Sir John A. Macdonald laid down the policy of this party when, speaking to the electors of Kingston on October 5, 1844, he made the following statement:
It is my firm belief that the prosperity of Canada depends upon its permanent connection with the mother country, and I shall resist to the utmost any attempt from whatever quarter to weaken that union.
Forty-seven years afterwards, speaking in February, 1891, in his last campaign during his last illness, he reaffirmed that doctrine, which has been the policy of every government since. On that occasion he said:
For a century and a half this country has grown and flourished under the protecting aegis of the British crown. Under the broad folds of the union jack, we enjoy the most ample liberty, we govern ourselves as we please, and at the same time we participate in the advantages which flow with association of the mightiest empire the world has ever seen. As for myself, my course is clear. A British subject I was born and a British subject I will die.
That has been the consistent policy of the Conservative party. Look at the record over the past fifty years and what do you find in regard to Canada's stand in the oceanic empire? In this war, all the dominions came forward unasked to the aid of the mother country, and the colonies, the mandated colonies, and the colonial empire including India, all volunteered their help. They have all done remarkable well, and Canada, as the senior dominion, holds an important key position between the United States and Britain.
In 1899 when the South African war broke out Canada played her part, small though it was. Apart from the war of 1812, that was the first contribution she had made to the mother country in waging a war. Canada raised, together with New Zealand and Australia, several hundred men who went to South Africa, and the British government paid all the costs. In the great war of 1914, the same thing happened ; the British fleet ensured the peace of world civilization for over 100 years. From 1815, for 100 years apart from one or two

In the South African war in 1899 there were in this country those people who said, "What have we to do with Britain's wars?" They contended that it was contrary to the constitution; it was against the British North America Act to send troops to South Africa. But the loyal people of the country-and fortunately they are not all in one party- brought pressure to bear upon the government of the day to send a contingent to South Africa, and compelled all governments from that day to this to take the stand that when Britain is at war Canada also is at war. They did the same in 1914, and the contribution that has been made to the mother country in this war has gone up by geometrical progression. There were three or four regiments in the South African war and in this war we have 600,000 or 700,000 men. And what we have done we have done voluntarily. What the dominions did in the two world wars has changed the whole history of the civilized world.
On Armistice day, 1918, there was great rejoicing throughout the world. People everywhere thought, with the close of the war, that there would be no more war, that the world had been made safe for democracy. Well, we, by pacifism and folly, lost all the benefits which the military forces had won in France and Flanders. The Germans saw to it that we did. The League of Nations was created and in 1922 was a going concern. During the years 1923, 1924, 1925, Britain completely disarmed; then came Locarno and with it the purchase of German favour, and after that 1936, when our empire ran down the toboggan and the British government allowed Germany to occupy the Rhine. In addition to that, in 1937, Britain and the United States stood aside and allowed Germany to occupy Austria, and in 1938 the frontiers of Czechoslovakia.

Then the deluge came and we found the British empire completely disarmed. That of course led to the war.
I have always supported the principle of a permanent empire council. Speaking in 1923 and again in 1924 and 1925, between the close of the first world war and the outbreak of the second, I urged on the attention of parliament the necessity for such a council. The last time I spoke was in November, 1941, as reported at page 4513 of daily Hansard. At that time I said that in my opinion the Prime Minister would have been well advised to support a permanent empire council and a war cabinet.' I said it was an absolute necessity and that New Zealand and Australia wanted it. He passed it up. Then came the fall of Singapore and Hong Kong, and I urged the government to call immediately a permanent empire council, because New Zealand and Australia, with Canada, could not any longer afford to have these decisions made against them without their consent and advice. So many hundreds of thousands of our young men could not fight without having something to say about it. This war, Mr. Speaker, will have been fought in vain and we shall have another war before the year 1970 or the close of this century unless we take advantage of the present conflict to carry into the peace some measure of collective security and the unity the dominions had in this war. That means an armed Britain and armed dominions. What does an unarmed Britain lead to? Invasion, insult and nearly in the end, extinction, as in this war.
In 1940 young men by the thousand went up in the air in the battle of London and Britain. By night and by day, twenty-four hours a day, these young airmen, some from the high schools of Toronto, played their part in this war in the air and saved Britain and civilization. Six hundred of them have been lost so far from the high schools in the city of Toronto alone. These young airmen in the battle of Britain have saved civilization. We owe to these young men everything we have in this country, and so do the people of Quebec, those of the maritimes and the people of the United States as well. But for these young men we would long ago have made peace with the axis powers. In view of the Prime Minister's stand, since he refuses to cooperate with New Zealand and Australia in the effort to secure a permanent empire council, it seems to me that Canada is at the parting of the ways. I am very much alarmed.
I submit that the time has come for the Prime Minister to tell the house what the foreign policy and empire policy of Canada

Where does Canada stand on the declaration of Churchill that he is not going to allow this empire to go into liquidation or go by default, because without the dominions Britain would be a second Denmark, and a second-class power. Mr. Curtin says conditions will never be the same in the Pacific as they were in 1939; therefore we must have the advantage of a concerted empire policy, which will have the power to stand for democracy in the southern Pacific in the post-war years. These will be complex years and Australia cannot afford to let her economic position be unknown and misunderstood. That should be the stand of Canada. Mr. Curtin said in a most notable speech in August, 1942, that Australia is proud of and completely satisfied with her status and rights as a self-governing member of the British commonwealth which is a partnership of equality and fraternity, a partnership whose history has been marked by great contributions to civilization.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the British commonwealth depends to a large extent on the stand which Canada takes. It will be too late when the prime ministers are meeting in England for Canada to declare her policy. We shall be back to where we were in 1937. We shall have no policy. It will be said we have no commitments; parliament will decide. It is a case of now or never; now and forever. Canada is a wonderful North American country of vast resoures and she has a stake in western Europe owing to the invention of the aeroplane. She has a stake also in the Atlantic region. Canada cannot be indifferent to European affairs if she is to be a great nation. Her destiny' requires her to be a leader in the commonwealth. Up to the beginning of this century Britain had to fear only naval power. Now she has to fear the aeroplane, and the whole world is changed.
The United States, that great nation which is allied with us in this war and has done so gloriously is the master of its own destiny. That is so, but it cannot interfere with Britain
and Canada having the closest ties. Canada's position is vital for the development of air communications, and these should be planned ahead of the prime ministers' meeting between Britain and Canada. It should be an all-empire, red-air policy. I referred at length to civil aviation on July 15 last, and received no reply from the government. Canada is a great country whose resources are vast. She should unite with New Zealand and Australia in a permanent empire council. The destiny of the empire lies largely in Canada's hands. Canada cannot go it alone or separately. We have had a treaty with the West Indies since 1912. Canada with Newfoundland and the West Indies should form a sort of regional council in the Atlantic for the future progress of the world. Canada is of great value to the world of the future as a member of the British commonwealth. After the war Canada should continue the good vrork she has done in this war and turn out to be an instrumeint for the keeping of peace in the world. If we do that we shall have captured our objective in this war and little more will be heard of war.
The government talks of equality of status and autonomy. It seems to me, with all these ambassadors going around the seven seas representing Britain and the dominions, we shall have nothing but a hidden Tower of Babel of ambassadors that we have at Washington and all the other capitals of the world. We shall come to be a nation of ambassadors. The government is so anxious about equality of status that it will not work with the other dominions in connection with foreign policy and empire policy, and has forgotten all about equality of function without which status is a myth. That is now up in the clouds. What is the use of us talking about Canada being a nation? The British empire, as Lord Balfour's committee said, is not founded on negations. It depends essentially, if not formally, on positive ideals. Free institutions are its lifeblood. Free cooperation is its instrument. Peace, security and progress are among its objectives. Cooperation within the empire for economic development is therefore absolutely necessary for the commonwealth and the colonial empire alike, and international cooperation in economic affairs would be far more difficult if the dominions be treated as separate units in international affairs.
Article 4 of the Atlantic charter safeguards imperial preference. There are many in Canada who do not realize that that principle is absolutely essential to the commonwealth if it is to exist and to the international status, not only to Britain but to the weaker members of the commonwealth. All the dominions will

lose their economic independence if the principle of economic unity within the empire is abrogated.
We have had a lot of talk in this country about this being a class war, a people's revolution and all that kind of thing, but between the two wars we did not hear a word from the pacifists about German imperialism and its menace to the world. What was the cause of this war? It was not for that reason at all. The people who are fighting this war are not fighting for any kind of political nostrum. That is not what the people of the devastated countries are fighting for or have suffered to death for. What caused this war was the determination of Germany to subjugate the continent of Europe so that by her army and military power she would control the people and the industries of Europe and thus have Britain and the British empire at her mercy. It is for that reason that the United States and all the other nations were attacked by Germany, and it is for that reason that Russia came into the war. There are some people who would like to substitute their own economic propaganda for the real German war, and who would like to substitute a political war of their own along certain lines. Imperial unity must be made our first task. We must recognize the fact that the empire can produce almost every article which Britain and her empire need for peace and war. Britain cannot go it alone without the dominions from which she must import twenty-five out of twenty-seven of her raw materials. With the dominions she is to be the greatest power in the world to-day.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there has been something said about parliamentary institutions and the supremacy of parliament. Criticism in time of war has stirred governments and cabinets to action on a number of matters belatedly and after a lot of urging. The functions of parliament have not changed from those first, days when in an historic speech to the sheriffs of Bristol, Burke made the statement that a member when he becomes a member does not become the representative only of the constituency he represents but of the country, as a whole, and that to be a good member was no easy task then or now if one does his duty, especially in a world war like this. One of the most important functions of a member is to criticize, to examine, to crossquestion the ministry and to debate not merely the policy of the government of the day, but more important the way the trust of administering the affairs of that country is conducted, and to act also as a check on expenditures and further taxation, and especially of examining - legislation.
IMr. Church.]
But if one consults the record of Hansard and the debates one will find that few avail themselves of such privileges. In this war what has happened? Outside boards have usurped the functions of parliament in a haphazard manner over parliament's head; privileges, powers and duties of a democratic parliament and of the ministers of the crown responsible for their actions have been usurped. The minister leaves it all to them with the result that parliament has surrendered and abdicated to those amateurs and overnight they have become experts. As a result legislation is left largely by parliament to the executive and the various control boards, and is carried through by orders in council. So we have these ghosts behind the scenes, these controllers who overnight become experts or bureaucrats and who, with little parliamentary criticism of their actions, pass laws simply because there is a war on. As I see it, to elect or reject governments is not one of the important functions of parliament; the people decide that. Nor is it one of the functions of parliament to propose legislation, since in nearly all cases that is laid down by the government of the day. Yet there never has been a time when it was more important that a useful and efficient private member should function, one who will consider the country's interests and the prosecution of the war as of primary importance, one who will ask questions in season and out of season, since it is in parliament alone that the real truth can be discovered and errors in administration exposed through the questioning and cross-questioning of ministers. In effect and in practice the supremacy of parliament in Canada is a myth. The real debates in this house in which the man on the street is interested rarely get beyond the walls of this building; they might as well be held in secret; yet this is the only place where anyone holding a grievance may have it remedied.
Such, in actual practice, is our new system of government in Canada; yet criticism here could restore the prestige of parliament and perhaps save the government from its friends. Since the beginning of this war, as for twenty years previously, I have urged that constitutional, parliamentary cabinet and law reform were Canada's principal domestic problems, and I have quoted authorities to support that statement; yet nothing has been done. Between the two wars Canada was the chief drifter from the empire. Our main empire interests should be defence, civil aviation, trade, foreign affairs and immigration within the empire, and that should start with British born immigration, and of soldiers first and those who won the battle of Britain, the people of the mother country, with assisted

The Address-Mr. Church
passages. They should be considered before we bring in any other continental people, though I have no objection to the principle to which one other hon. member referred to-day.
As I have said, Canada was the chief drifter from the empire. At the imperial conferences of 1927 and 1937 we refused to cooperate with our sister dominions of Australia and New Zealand in the matters I have mentioned, on the ground that we had no commitments and that parliament would decide, which, as I have said, was a myth. Canada relied on various peace pacts, agreements, pacifism, the Monroe doctrine and all that kind of thing. We threw away our defences on land, sea and in the air; we lost our friends, and in 1937, when urged by Australia and New Zealand to support an empire air scheme, an empire shipping policy and rearmament for collective security, we refused to do so. The government has conducted a Liberal war in many ways, though many very fine things have been done in connection with munitions and food, and particularly in regard to assistance to Britain, which was a splendid action on our part. However, our man-power policy in my opinion has been carried on by fits and starts, with nothing being continued for very long and no equality of either service or of sacrifice. We have no foreign policy; we never had any policy but drift. We have no empire policy, which is the most important of all. Every year I have urged the creation of an empire council to bring about a wise modem system of empire collaboration, consultation and cooperation between Britain, her dominions and colonies and mandated areas. After the fall of Singapore and Hong Kong in 1941, I urged in this house that a permanent empire tribunal be set up, with a permanent secretariat, to meet frequently and decide all empire matters, since Britain cannot exist without the dominions. Mr. Curtin was right in advocating such a plan, and I am sorry that we have not followed him.
In this war Britain and her dominions, alone, saved the world for two years, and saved civilization from being destroyed. The day of isolation in Canada is gone forever. The great dominions should hang together and have unity in action, while retaining their status and sovereignty and autonomy. They can still combine to aid the mother country and the empire but, unless they are united, each will hang by itself, since none is strong enough to go it alone as a separate nation. Britain and her dominions, while willing to aid in rebuilding a better world and allowing the free use of all raw materials, as far as possible, should retain sovereignty over the 100-8
empire and not lose any of her territory. In this war the loyalty of all the dominions and colonies, and of India, has been shown to a striking degree, as was the case in the last war. But the various parts of the empire should meet as one unit to discuss matters of defence, collective security, civil aviation and so on. While we are always paying great tribute to our allies and working in unison with them, I believe that since this war began parliament has missed a great opportunity each session to discuss for several days primary empire problems. Each session we have been able to discuss the price of wheat for four or five weeks; yet only for part of a day toward the end of the session are we permitted to discuss the important matters of foreign affairs, empire unity, and so on, which will be the salvation of this country. The mother country should be the axis of the empire, and should give leadership. Empire affairs should be prominent in our parliaments, and frequent meetings should be held between representatives of the parliaments of the empire for consultation, collaboration and cooperation in a forward empire policy of progress leading to a better world after this war.
Christianity is part and parcel of our empire; indeed, the empire is founded on Christianity. This principle was reasserted to the people of India by Queen Victoria in 1858, when the British government took over the Indian empire. The British empire is Christian, not in a sectarian sense but because a Christian people founded and developed it, and it has been Christian in all its institutions ever since. We assert the individual right of the human soul and of all faiths; that all have equal rights as long as they are humane. The kindred nations of our empire have had a record of which they may be proud, for their service to humanity, justice, freedom, civilization and progress. The British empire will continue, after this war, to have a leading place in the service of the world and of mankind.

In my opening remarks, Mr. Speaker, I should like to put what I consider the first thing first. When we realize that every member of this house has been spared to come back and serve here I believe it is our duty to express our thanks to the Supreme Being for having allowed us to carry on.
When I think of the speech from the throne I think of the judgment shown by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) when he was casting about for brilliant men to move and

The Address-Mr. Mclvor

second the address. He came all the way across to this comer of the chamber, and I am sure we in this loyal corner feel greatly honoured that he should wander over here to select two brilliant minds for this task. I doubt if he could have found two hon. members in any part of the house who would have served better. Both hon. gentlemen are soldiers; both are honourable men; both have brilliant minds, and are men who think for themselves under all circumstances.
As I read and re-read the speech from the throne and then went back and re-read the Marsh report and the Beveridge report, together with the findings of Doctor James, I must say that in my judgment the speech from the throne is the cream of them all. It is the best thing I have seen; it holds the greatest promise of a reconstruction plan. It suits me immensely. I am one of those who demanded, as far as I could, a programme for reconstruction, and we have a right to be grateful to those who have given us this programme. Of course I know that we agree with it or disagree with it, according to the group in the house to which we belong. I appreciated the observations of the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Roebuck) who gave us a clear view of our duty as a dominion toward those who have been wronged and driven from their homes. He has told us our duty toward those refugees. I am not a bit particular whether the men, women and children are Jews or Gentiles, whether they are red, black or yellow. They are made in the image of their Creator, and they belong to the type of people for whom Christ died. I am sure we as a nation are not going to play the role of the priest and the Levite who walked by on the other side, and allow those who are in distress to suffer. I agree with the hon. member for Trinity when he says that we should do our best for those people. I say that 111 in one year is not enough. In the words of the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) which he uses frequently; it is not good enough.
There are certain features of the speech from the throne which stand out, and which suit me very well. Family allowances have been subjected to some criticism. In my view this measure has been long overdue. When I think of the Prime Minister, denied the happiness of a family of sis or eight or ten to welcome him home at night, and remember that he is helping to put this plan across, and that it is his suggestion for reconstruction, I am convinced that it shows the marks of a great mind. If I were an employer of labour and a man came to me for employment, telling me that he had a wife and nothing else,

and if at the same time another man came, telling me that he had a wife and six children, I would think that the man with the children would do a bigger and a better job and would be more entitled to consideration than the one who had no children, and perhaps no home at all.
Another point which stands out in the speech from the throne is the housing plan. I do not know anything that would mean more employment for more people than would be the construction of buildings. Certainly those build- ings are needed throughout Canada. We at the head of the lakes, with our abundance of timber which can be cut down and manufactured into lumber, are of the opinion that this housing programme would be a great boon to the Thunder Bay district.
Then, as I look ahead I can see the minister of reconstruction. Of course hon. members may imagine who I think would be the best qualified for that job. I can see him working with an industrial bank close to hand, for his own special use and, in my opinion, such an industrial bank would be a good thing.
Another matter which is of interest to the owner of a farm is the floor price for staple farm products. I have gone to farmers and bought eggs for as little as fifteen cents a dozen. They were glad to get that price. And when we think of farmers raising fowl, and think of all the care required in that operation, and then realize that they have had to sell their eggs for as little as ten cents or fifteen cents a dozen, we must hope that that may never happen again. The farmers are entitled to this new law.
I now come to a subject which is dear to me, namely that of labour. The new labour code has not yet been published, but it is my hope that it will contain a provision for compulsory bargaining. I know it would be better if it were not necessary to have the compulsory provision; but in my opinion such a provision is absolutely necessary for the good of production and of management, and is in the best interests of directors. Certainly it is in the interest of labour.
Then I should hope that under the new code labour would receive holidays with pay. When I see a man toiling twelve months in a year in a machine shop I am bound to conclude that he needs holidays with pay far more than the young man who spends perhaps only eight hours or seven and a half hours in an office. The office worker may work from 9 until 12 o'clock noon, and from 1.30 until 5.30 p.m. Or, let us consider the man who works in a mine. He works deep in the earth, away from the sunlight, and breathes different air. Do hon.

The Address-Mr. Mclvor
members not think he is more entitled to holidays with pay than even a member of parliament, no matter what position he occupies?
I shall reserve any criticism I may have to make until the new labour code is brought down. However, I should like to bring to the attention of those who are responsible the fact that I have received letters from secretaries of labour unions in which they have dealt with war-time wage control order P.C. 9384. These are the words of H. Rember, secretary for local 132:
We the members of local 132 feel that wartime wages control order P.C. 9384 when put into effect would destroy the democratic right of workers to bargain collectively.
Also it is pointed out that this order would hurt labour at the present time. I believe the secretary makes a mistake when he says that hon. members should intercede on their behalf in the hope that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) may not permit this order to become effective. I do not think the minister has much to do with the order. He may know about it, but it is not his order-and I shall stand corrected if I am wrong. I do not think the Minister of Labour has fathered everything considered wrong by labour unions.
May I ^ say that I know these unions, and the men in them. They are just as honest as we are. I stand side by side with them in striving to help them get the best possible returns for the energy they put into their work. I have not found them selfish. On the contrary they are straight, honest workers, and I would advise that reconsideration be given this order, and that something better be substituted.
Those who are making reforms might consider the use of the transferable vote. In a single constituency there may be four or five men. and perhaps one lady in a campaign. If there is no transferable vote the result would be that many people would not be represented at all, and for that reason I urge that those who are considering reforms might consider the adoption of the transferable vote.
There is another point I have in mind, one which I might not understand as clearly as I should. I find that the educational facilities in Canada cannot be embraced by certain types of people. There are young men and maidens in outlying districts who do not have the advantage of advanced education. In mv view the federal government should put itseif on record as being willing to cooperate with departments of education in the provinces to make it possible for these young people, who are keen to acquire education, to secure the degree of education they may desire.
I have a suggestion to offer to the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. 100-8i
Mackenzie). There should be an amendment to the Pension Act, and in this connection I should like to give one or two examples. I know of one man who enlisted in the ail force. He was not there very long before he took what is commonly known as polio. He may not have got the attention he should have received, and to-day he finds himself a hopeless cripple for life. Because he was not long enough in the force he is not eligible for a pension. It is true that he received treatment, and I pay tribute to the doctors at the Deer Lodge hospital for the splendid treatment they gave him, but the fact is that he is not able to get further education without going back to school at the expense of his father and mother. The pension he was receiving has been reduced to $25 a month.
Another young man was in the navy when he was taken down with tuberculosis, perhaps partly owing to neglect. They did not think his case was as serious as it proved to be. He probably will be weakened for the rest of his life. These two men have not got what I consider is their due, and I bring their cases to the attention of the minister.
I join with others who have paid a tribute to the young men who have gone overseas, particularly to those who played hockey, rugby and basketball. I have always taken a keen interest in these games and some of these boys played under me. I receive letters from these boys in which they say, "We are just giving the enemy the same thing we tried to give the opposing team when you were in the sub box.' Some of these young fellows will not come back, and others are having a terrific time, especially those on the corvettes on the high seas. But I do not think they are having a harder time than the fathers and mothers who receive word of loved ones who are missing and then the final news thal they must be considered dead. I have been in many homes, and I consider it most courageous on the part of mothers and fathers who have lost loved ones when they go out and carry on and help others in the same difficult position.
I have my own way of looking at things just as other men have according to their occupations. I think this country is reaching a position for which it will pay dearly in the future. Sunday work is prevalent all over Canada. Some of us have struggled for the preservation of one day in seven, and I have no patience with any man, whether he be a member of parliament or otherwise, who will use the Sabbath for anything but rest and worship. One time I saw a picture depicting the theme that if you break the ten com-
The Address-Mr. Mclvor

mandments, the ten commandments will break you. I think it was Gladstone who said, and I like to quote the grand-old man, that righteousness exalteth a nation but sin is a reproach to any people. He said that it was a sad day when we neglected our Sabbath day.
We hear a good deal to-day about juvenile delinquency. It is said that it is on the increase everywhere because there is so much money to spend. I have not my facts before me, but I am convinced by reports that juvenile delinquency in Fort William is not nearly as bad as it was during the depression. In those days I have seen as many as twenty boys in the police court at one time. During this last year there has been very little juvenile delinquency.
I do not know who is responsible for the king's honours, but I do commend the Prime Minister for being very sparing in recommending these honours. I think they should be given to our soldiers, and in this connection I should like to refer to one of the finest armies we have in Canada-the Salvation Army. They are always on the attack, not on the defence. They are on the attack against wrong, and those who are responsible for recommending the king's honours should consider some of these outstanding soldiers because they are doing a great job.
Those soldiers who come back from the front should take care to report to the representative of the department of pensions, the pensions advocate. Right here I should like to pay a tribute to the employment officials in the Canadian Car. I recall one case of a young fellow who had been dismissed from this company for bad conduct. He served with a tank corps in north Africa for some time and when he came back he wanted to get work with the Canadian Car. However, the superintendent of employment said that he did not want him. We then said to him, "Do you not think that a boy who has served in the tanks and has fought for your protection should be given some consideration; should you not be willing to forgive him a good deal?" He said, "We will forgive him and take him back." That is the sort of treatment the management of the Canadian Car in Fort William are giving to the returned men.
There are certain things that we need in Fort William, and there are certain suggestions I should like to make to the committee on reconstruction. The first is the necessity for the building up of the home. The home is the most important institution in the community. If you have a poor home, you have a poor community. Many of us have had the blessing of a good home; we have been trained
TMr. Mclvor.]
to do the things that we should do-oftentimes we have wandered far-but we think a family altar should be built in every home. The committee on reconstruction should consider that.
I realize that men and women are needed for war work, but I do say that the place of a mother with children is not in the workshop where she is earning money; she should be at home building up character, making her boys and girls fit to go out and take their places as honourable Christian citizens.
As I say, there are certain things we need in Fort William. I am going to hurry up with my remarks because, if I do not finish now, I shall have to complete my speech when the budget is before us. The minister of pensions knows that at the present time the outstanding need of Fort William is an up-to-date hospital, not only for the old folks and the returned soldiers but for the city at large. The Department of National Defence took away our skating and hockey rink. We need an ice rink now. We need a new home for the army and navy veterans, and there are other public buildings that should be erected. I am going to present these claims to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) and ask for money at a low rate of interest.
The shell factory in Fort William was closed down. The workers were greatly disappointed because they had been happy in their work. There had been a particularly fine type of management there. However, all those who wanted to go to work were offered positions with the Canadian Car and many of them took them. The work being carried out by the Canadian Car is very good. There are 6,052 people working there, 3,285 men and 1,875 women with a considerable office staff. The production of the Curtis dive bomber is now one a day which speaks well for Canadian Car and Foundry company, because they had many setbacks.
When we think of what we have in the district of Thunder Bay, which includes Port Arthur and Fort William, when we remember that one of the outstanding things with which we are confronted is that the haematite ore from Steep Rock will be coming down and will have to be shipped some place else, we believe that we should have a plant where that ore can be smelted and the product, after it has been refined, shipped out. It is all right to ship our pulp across the line; our United States friends can make use of it. But I do not agree that our iron ore should be shipped across the line; I think it should be handled at the head of the lakes where we have any amount of power and water and timber, as well as the workers who will be needed.

Regarding the needs of labour at the present time, I feel confident that we may leave the cause of the worker in the hands of the government, because it is not a matter for the Minister of Labour alone; it is the responsibility of the whole government.
I had a good deal more to say, but I have decided, in view of requests which have been made, to finish my speech when the budget is brought down. I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for your consideration.
